lessons.title: Finding the argument

steps.headline: An argument is a claim with reasons offered for it.

lead.text: The claim you are asked to accept is the conclusion. The claims offered as reasons for it are the premises.
Indicator words help: “since”, “because” and “after all” introduce a premise, while “so” and “thus” signal a conclusion.
Position does not decide it. A conclusion can come first, last or in the middle.
Standard form lists each premise on its own line, then the conclusion. That lets you judge the support before you argue about whether the premises are true.
A single clause can carry more than one claim, joined by “and”.

reveal.text: You just separated the reasons from the claim they back. Writing each premise on its own line, then the conclusion, is standard form.

model.passage: Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.

premises.text: The bridge was built before 1950.
Every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year.

conclusion.text: The bridge must be inspected this year.

model.passage: The vote is not valid, for the quorum is twelve members and only nine attended.

premises.text: The quorum for a valid vote is twelve members.
Only nine members attended the vote.

conclusion.text: The vote is not valid.

steps.headline: Find the argument in: “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.”

workedSteps.text: Ask what the passage wants you to believe. That is the conclusion: we should not repaint yet.
“After all” announces that reasons follow. List them: the roof still leaks, and new paint would be spoiled.
Write it in standard form.
workedSteps.math: P1: The roof still leaks. P2: New paint would be spoiled. C: We shouldn't repaint the hall yet.

steps.headline: Find the conclusion in the council's passage about the playing field.

workedSteps.text: Look for the word that announces reasons: “after all”.
Ask which sentence the others are there to support.
The two reasons after “after all” become P1 and P2.

model.passage: The council should not sell the playing field. After all, it is the only open space in the ward, and selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's own planning policy.

premises.text: The playing field is the only open space in the ward.
Selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's planning policy.

conclusion.text: The council should not sell the playing field.

model.passage: You will be late to the meeting: the 8:10 has been cancelled, and the next train arrives after it starts.

premises.text: The 8:10 train has been cancelled.
The next train arrives after the meeting starts.

conclusion.text: You will be late for the meeting.

lead.text: Speakers often skip a premise they think is obvious. To find it, ask what else must be true for the stated reason to support the conclusion.

reveal.text: That missing premise is the bridge. An argument with one left unstated is an enthymeme, from a term in Aristotle's Rhetoric. Supplying it can expose a weak spot: many solicitors qualified after a degree in another subject.

model.passage: Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree.

premises.text: Every solicitor has a law degree.
Mira is a solicitor.

conclusion.text: Mira has a law degree.

model.passage: The kettle is switched on at the wall, yet the water is cold after five minutes. So the kettle is broken.

premises.text: If the kettle is switched on at the wall and works, it heats the water.
The kettle is switched on at the wall.
The water is cold after five minutes.

conclusion.text: The kettle does not work.

lead.text: Long arguments often chain. A claim drawn on the way and then used as a premise for the next step is an intermediate conclusion.
Mapping the chain shows where an objection would bite.

model.passage: Water expands when it freezes, so a full, sealed glass bottle left in the freezer will crack; and a cracked bottle leaks, so the freezer will need cleaning.

premises.text: A full, sealed glass bottle of water will crack in the freezer.
A cracked bottle leaks.

conclusion.text: The freezer will need cleaning.

model.passage: Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.

premises.text: The bridge was built before 1950.
Every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year.

conclusion.text: The bridge must be inspected this year.

lessons.title: Valid, sound and counterexamples

steps.headline: An argument is valid when no possible situation has true premises and a false conclusion.

lead.text: Validity is about the link between premises and conclusion, whatever the facts are.
A situation with true premises and a false conclusion is a counterexample. One counterexample is enough to show an argument invalid.
Read “if … then” as a promise: when the first part holds, the second must. It does not say the first part is the only way to get the second.
Look for a different way the pavement could be wet.

reveal.text: You went looking for a counterexample, and one exists: a burst water main wets the pavement on a dry night. This pattern is called affirming the consequent. Its neighbour, modus ponens, has no such situation.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
The pavement is wet.

conclusion.text: It rained overnight.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It rained overnight.

conclusion.text: The pavement is wet.

steps.headline: Test the form p → q, p, so q with a truth table.

workedSteps.text: List every way p and q can be true or false. Two letters give four rows.
Keep the rows where both premises are true. The premise p needs p true, and p → q is false when q is false.
One row remains, with p and q both true. The conclusion q is true there, so no counterexample exists. The form is valid.

steps.headline: Test the form p → q, q, so p with a truth table.

workedSteps.text: List the four rows for p and q.
Keep the rows where both premises are true.
Look at the conclusion p in those rows. If p is false in one of them, that row is a counterexample.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
The pavement is wet.

conclusion.text: It rained overnight.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
The pavement is not wet.

conclusion.text: It did not rain overnight.

lead.text: Validity ignores whether the premises are true. A sound argument is valid and has only true premises.
Check each premise against the facts.

reveal.text: You checked the facts, and validity never needed them. If both premises were true the conclusion would have to be, so the argument is valid. A false premise makes it unsound.

premises.text: All metals are magnetic.
Copper is a metal.

conclusion.text: Copper is magnetic.

premises.text: All mammals breathe air.
Whales are mammals.

conclusion.text: Whales breathe air.

lead.text: Each extra atomic sentence doubles the rows. Three letters give eight.
Do not list them all. Start from the conclusion: p → r fails in only some rows. Then ask what the premises need there.

premises.text: If the alarm sounds, the guard wakes.
If the guard wakes, the gate is locked.

conclusion.text: If the alarm sounds, the gate is locked.

premises.text: If the alarm sounds, the guard wakes.
If the gate is locked, the guard wakes.

conclusion.text: If the alarm sounds, the gate is locked.

lessons.orientation: Test validity by searching for a counterexample row, and separate a valid argument from a sound one.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: At the party, every guest was given a badge. Priya was a guest.

intro.whyItMatters: A strong-sounding argument can still be broken, and a counterexample is the quickest way to show it.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when no possible situation makes every premise true and the conclusion false. It is sound when it is also valid and has true premises.

blocks.text: You found a counterexample to the rain argument, counted the rows where both premises held, and saw that the magnetic-metals argument is valid yet unsound.

lessons.title: Fallacies and charity

steps.headline: A fallacy is a pattern of reasoning that looks convincing but fails.

lead.text: Two common ones are worth knowing first. Begging the question assumes the conclusion in a premise. A false dilemma offers two options when more exist.
Dr Okafor's load calculations can be checked whatever her history with the firm. Ask whether the reply engages with her reasons or with something else.

reveal.text: You separated the argument from the arguer. Rejecting an argument because of who offers it is the ad hominem fallacy.

premises.text: Dr Okafor says the bridge design is unsafe.
Dr Okafor once lost a contract to the design firm.

conclusion.text: Her claim that the design is unsafe can be dismissed.

premises.text: The only support for the claim is an anonymous source's say-so.
The source profits if the rival design is chosen.

conclusion.text: The claim needs independent confirmation before we rely on it.

steps.headline: Sam: “We should add a bike lane on Mill Road.” Kit: “Sam wants to ban cars from the town.” Is Kit's reply fair?

workedSteps.text: Restate what Sam proposed: one bike lane, on one road.
Restate what Kit attacks: a ban on cars across the whole town.
Kit refutes a more extreme position that Sam never held. That move is called a straw man.

steps.headline: Ana proposes 20 mph beside schools. Ben criticises a national 20 mph limit. What has Ben done?

workedSteps.text: Restate Ana's proposal: a lower limit on roads beside schools.
Restate what Ben criticises: every car in the country crawling at 20.
Name the move.

premises.text: Ana wants every car in the country to drive at 20 mph.
A national 20 mph limit would badly damage the economy.

conclusion.text: Ana's proposal should be rejected.

premises.text: Ana proposes a 20 mph limit on roads beside schools.
Buses on those roads would then miss their timetables.

conclusion.text: Ana's proposal needs a change to the bus timetables.

lead.text: Check whether each key word means the same thing in every premise. If it shifts, the argument only looks valid because the word stays the same.

reveal.text: You checked the word, not the logic. Equivocation shifts the meaning of a word between premises: here “light” means “not heavy” and then “pale”.

premises.text: A feather is light.
Whatever is light is not dark.

conclusion.text: A feather is not dark.

premises.text: The robbers met at the bank.
A bank is the side of a river.

conclusion.text: The robbers met beside a river.

lead.text: The principle of charity asks you to rebuild an argument in its most plausible form before you judge it. Answering a weaker version would be a straw man of your own.
Choose the added premise a thoughtful speaker would accept.

reveal.text: The believable premise makes the argument valid and worth answering. The others are false or far stronger than the speaker needs.

model.passage: Smoking causes cancer, so you shouldn't smoke.

premises.text: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease.
Smoking greatly raises the risk of lung cancer.

conclusion.text: You should not smoke.

premises.text: Either the council closes the library or the council goes bankrupt.
The council must not go bankrupt.

conclusion.text: The council must close the library.

lessons.orientation: Name common informal fallacies and reconstruct an opponent's argument in its most plausible form.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Jo says the school canteen should serve more vegetables. Her neighbour replies: “Jo's a vegetarian, so ignore her.”

intro.promise: By the end you'll name common fallacies when you meet them and rebuild an opponent's argument in its strongest form before you reply.
intro.whyItMatters: Most bad arguments make a familiar slip, and a name makes the slip easy to point at.

recap.keyIdea: Name the slip, then answer the best version. Fallacies hide in who says it, what was answered, shifting words, circles and false choices, and charity means rebuilding the argument fairly first.

blocks.text: You separated a reply about a person from a reply about reasons, caught a swapped proposal and a shifting word, then chose the most charitable premise.

lessons.title: Knowledge and Gettier cases

steps.headline: On the traditional view, knowledge is justified true belief.

lead.text: S knows that p when three things hold. p is true. S believes p. S is justified in believing p.
A lucky guess is believed and true but unjustified. A false claim cannot be known at all.
Judge truth against what actually happened, not against Smith's evidence. Judge justification by his reasons at the moment he formed the belief.

reveal.text: All three conditions hold, yet his evidence was about Jones while the fact that makes his belief true is about himself. Edmund Gettier used a case like this in 1963 to argue that the conditions can hold while the belief is true only by luck.

model.subject: Smith
model.belief: The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.
model.evidence: The company president told him Jones will get the job; he counted ten coins in Jones's pocket.
model.fact: Smith gets the job, and Smith happens to have ten coins in his own pocket.

model.subject: Ravi
model.evidence: He looks out of the window and sees rain falling on the street.
model.fact: It is raining, and the rain is what he sees.

steps.headline: Ravi looks out of the window, sees rain falling and believes it is raining. Does he know?

workedSteps.text: True? Yes, it is raining.
Believed and justified? Yes. He believes it, and he can see it.
Here the justification is connected to the fact: the rain is what he sees.
So the analysis gives knowledge, and so does intuition.

steps.headline: Ana reads a usually reliable station clock showing 2:15. It is 2:15, but the clock stopped twelve hours ago.

workedSteps.text: True? Yes, it is 2:15.
Believed and justified? Yes. Reading a usually reliable clock is a good reason.
Apply the analysis.

model.subject: Ana
model.evidence: The station clock, usually reliable, reads 2:15.
model.fact: It is 2:15, but the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago.

model.subject: Ravi
model.evidence: He looks out of the window and sees rain falling on the street.
model.fact: It is raining, and the rain is what he sees.

lead.text: A condition is necessary when knowledge cannot exist without it. It is sufficient when having it guarantees knowledge.

reveal.text: Gettier's Ford case works the same way: Smith validly infers a disjunction from a well-supported false belief, and it is true by coincidence. One reply, no-false-lemmas, adds a fourth condition: the reasoning must not pass through a false belief.

model.subject: Smith
model.belief: Either Jones owns a Ford or Brown is in Barcelona.
model.evidence: Jones has always driven a Ford and has just offered Smith a ride in one.
model.fact: Jones rents the car and owns no Ford; by chance, Brown is in Barcelona.

model.subject: Smith
model.belief: The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.
model.evidence: The company president told him Jones will get the job; he counted ten coins in Jones's pocket.
model.fact: Smith gets the job, and Smith happens to have ten coins in his own pocket.

lead.text: Carl Ginet's fake-barn case, published by Alvin Goldman in 1976, has no false step in the reasoning to blame. Henry sees a real barn in a county full of barn facades.
Ask what Henry would have believed had he glanced at another building.

reveal.text: Henry's belief is not safe: it could easily have been false. Safety and reliability conditions explain why he lacks knowledge, whereas no-false-lemmas, which blames a false belief in the reasoning, does not.

model.subject: Henry
model.evidence: He sees a barn clearly from the road in good light.
model.fact: It is the one real barn in a county full of barn facades.

model.subject: Ana
model.evidence: The station clock, usually reliable, reads 2:15.
model.fact: It is 2:15, but the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago.

intro.whyItMatters: Knowing is more than being right. Gettier cases show how luck can hide inside a good reason.

recap.keyIdea: Knowledge needs more than a true belief with good reasons. Gettier cases show that the three conditions can hold while the belief is true only by luck.

blocks.text: You checked Smith, Ravi and Ana against the three conditions, and saw that Ravi's evidence connects to the fact while Smith's and Ana's do not.

lessons.title: Dreams, demons and closure

steps.headline: A sceptical hypothesis says things seem as they do but are not.

lead.text: Descartes's example is an all-powerful deceiver, a demon. Dreams show that the senses can fool us. The demon could fool us about much more.
Yet to be deceived at all, Descartes must exist.
The modern sceptic turns the demon into a short argument. Test its shape as you would any argument: look for a case where both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

reveal.text: You tested the shape. The form is modus tollens, which has no counterexample row, so the argument is valid. A reply has to reject a premise.

premises.text: If I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived by a demon.
I do not know I am not deceived by a demon.

conclusion.text: I do not know I have hands.

premises.text: If I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived by a demon.
I know I have hands.

conclusion.text: I know I am not deceived by a demon.

steps.headline: In 1939 G. E. Moore held up his hands. How can his argument and the sceptic's both be valid?

The sceptic starts from “I do not know I am not deceived”. Moore starts from “I know I have hands”.
Each reaches the opposite conclusion. Moore found his hands more certain than any philosophical premise against them.

lead.text: Dretske and Nozick accept that you know you have hands. They deny that you can know you are not a handless brain in a vat.
Ask which general principle about knowledge those two verdicts contradict.

reveal.text: That principle is closure: if you know p, and know that p entails q, you know q. The sceptic's first premise is an instance of it. Their price: knowing you have hands without being able to know you are not envatted.

I do not know I am not a handless brain in a vat.

lessons.title: Evidence and credence

steps.headline: Evidence moves a belief from a prior to a posterior.

lead.text: Your prior is how likely a hypothesis was before the evidence. Your posterior is how likely it is after.
Bayes' theorem links them: P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) / P(E). Counting people gives the same answer more simply.
Picture the 1,000 people in two groups, the ill and the well. The test flags people in both.
Of everyone who is flagged, ask how many are ill.

reveal.text: You counted the positives from both groups. A positive result leaves a 50% chance of illness, far below the test's 90% hit rate.

steps.headline: A test catches 80% of cases and flags 5% of healthy people. 20% of 1,000 people have the condition. What share of positives are ill?

workedSteps.text: Split the 1,000 people.
Count the positives in each group.
Divide the ill positives by all positives.

steps.headline: The same 90% hit rate and 10% false alarms, now on a condition that affects 1% of 1,000 people.

reveal.text: A positive result now means illness only 9 times in 108, about 8%. Judging a test by its hit rate while ignoring how rare the condition is, is called base-rate neglect.

workedSteps.text: Find how many people are ill, and how many of them the test catches.
Apply the false-alarm rate to everyone who is well, and add the two groups of positives.

lead.text: Bayes' theorem has an odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. The likelihood ratio compares how probable the evidence is if H is true with how probable it is if H is false.

reveal.text: A 10% prior is odds of 1 to 9. Multiplying by the ratio gives even odds, which is 50%. A 1% prior is 1 to 99, and the same test lifts it only to 9 to 99.

lead.text: Change one number at a time and recount. Here the test is weaker at catching cases but gives fewer false alarms, and the condition affects one person in ten.

reveal.text: Lowering false alarms usually does more for a rare condition than raising the hit rate, because most positives then come from the healthy group.

blocks.text: In a town of 1,000 people, 100 have a condition. A test flags 90 of those 100. It also flags 90 of the 900 people who do not have it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll update a belief by counting people, and explain why a good test can mislead for a rare condition.
intro.whyItMatters: Medical tests, forecasts and news all hand you evidence. Counting is how you weigh it.

recap.keyIdea: Evidence does not settle a belief alone. How far a positive result moves you depends on how common the hypothesis was, so count both groups.

blocks.text: You counted 90 ill and 90 well people among the positives, saw the same test fall to about 8% when the condition was rare, and found the factor of 9.

lessons.title: Mind and body

steps.headline: If A and B are one thing, whatever is true of A is true of B.

lead.text: This is Leibniz's law. It lets you prove that two names pick out different things: find a property that one has and the other lacks.
Take care, though. “Being believed by Lois to fly” describes Lois's mind, not the man.
In the story, Superman and Clark Kent are one man. Check whether the premises can both be true in that story while the conclusion is false.

reveal.text: True premises with a false conclusion is a counterexample, so the argument is invalid. “Being believed by Lois to fly” is not a property of the man, so Leibniz's law cannot carry it across. “Being doubted by me” may be the same.

premises.text: I can doubt that my body exists.
I cannot doubt that I exist.
If A is identical with B, whatever is true of A is true of B.

conclusion.text: I am not identical with my body.

premises.text: Lois believes that Superman can fly.
Lois does not believe that Clark Kent can fly.
If A is identical with B, whatever is true of A is true of B.

conclusion.text: Superman is not Clark Kent.

steps.headline: Descartes: I can doubt that my body exists, but I cannot doubt that I exist. So I am not my body. Does it work?

workedSteps.text: Premise 1: my body has the property of being doubted by me. Premise 2: I lack that property, since I cannot doubt that I exist.
Leibniz's law: if I were my body, whatever is true of one would be true of the other.
So I am not my body. This stands only if “being doubted by me” is a real property, which the masked man puts in question.

lead.text: In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked Descartes how a mind with no extension could move a body that has it.
Ask what to call her challenge.

reveal.text: That is the interaction problem: how two substances with nothing in common could causally affect each other. Descartes compared the mind's action to heaviness, and she was not persuaded.

steps.headline: Test Elisabeth's argument with a truth table.

lead.text: Let p be “the mind moves the body”, q “it touches the body” and r “the mind is extended”. Her premises are p → q, q → r and ¬r. Her conclusion is ¬p.

workedSteps.text: Three letters give eight rows.
Count the rows where all three premises are true.
Check the conclusion ¬p in those rows. If it holds in all of them, the argument is valid.

premises.text: If the mind moves the body, it touches the body.
If the mind touches the body, it is extended.
The mind is not extended.

conclusion.text: The mind does not move the body.

premises.text: I can doubt that my body exists.
I cannot doubt that I exist.
If A is identical with B, whatever is true of A is true of B.

conclusion.text: I am not identical with my body.

lead.text: Physicalism holds that everything, minds included, is physical. One physicalist answer says that each type of mental state, such as pain, just is a type of brain state, as lightning is electrical discharge.

reveal.text: That is the identity theory, proposed by U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart in the 1950s. A weaker view, property dualism, keeps one physical substance but says mental properties are not physical properties.

premises.text: Every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause.
Some mental events cause physical events.
Those physical events are not caused twice over.

conclusion.text: Those mental events are physical events.

premises.text: If the mind moves the body, it touches the body.
If the mind touches the body, it is extended.
The mind is not extended.

conclusion.text: The mind does not move the body.

lessons.orientation: Assess Descartes' case for dualism, Elisabeth's interaction problem and the physicalist alternatives.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Sam is the mayor. Your friend believes Sam is a good cook, and has no view about whether the mayor is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test Descartes' argument for dualism with Leibniz's law, state Elisabeth's objection and name the physicalist alternatives.
intro.whyItMatters: Whether the mind is more than the brain shapes how we think about machines, medicine and ourselves.

recap.keyIdea: Leibniz's law can prove two things distinct, but only for real properties. Descartes' doubt argument is shaky for that reason, and Elisabeth's valid argument leaves dualists a premise to deny.

blocks.text: You found that the masked-man argument fails and set Descartes' doubt argument beside it. Then you checked Elisabeth's argument row by row.

recap.nextHook: If the mind is what the brain does, could another machine have one? Next, functionalism and the Chinese Room.

lessons.title: Function and the Chinese Room

steps.headline: A functional state is defined by what it does, not what it is made of.

lead.text: A machine table gives, for each state and input, the next state and the output. In Ned Block's drinks machine, “10p credited” is whatever state turns a further 10p into a can.
Nothing in the table mentions gears or chips.
Block's machine sells a can for 20p and starts with nothing owed. From nothing owed, a 10p moves it to 10p credited with no output. From 10p credited, a 10p buys a can and returns it to nothing owed.

reveal.text: You ran the table: credit, can, credit again. The state “10p credited” is just whatever role it plays in the next move.

steps.headline: Run the machine on 10p, 20p, 10p from nothing owed. What has come out, and where does it end?

workedSteps.text: 10p from nothing owed: the machine moves to 10p credited. Nothing comes out.
20p with 10p credited: it pays for a can and returns 10p. The machine goes back to nothing owed.
10p again: it moves to 10p credited. In all, one can and 10p change have come out.

steps.headline: Start with nothing owed and insert 20p, then 10p, then 20p.

workedSteps.text: 20p with nothing owed buys a can at once.
10p sets up a credit.
Count the cans after the last coin.

lead.text: In 1967 Hilary Putnam argued that pain might occur in humans, in an octopus with a very different nervous system and, in principle, in silicon. If pain were one particular brain state, creatures without it could not feel pain.

reveal.text: That is multiple realisability: the same table can be implemented by gears, neurons or chips, so the same mental kind can have many physical realisers.

lead.text: In 1980 John Searle imagined himself in a room, matching incoming Chinese characters to outgoing ones by an English rulebook. To people outside, the room converses fluently. Searle understands no Chinese.
If not in the man, where might the understanding be?

reveal.text: The systems reply says the whole room understands. Searle answers that he could memorise the rules and still understand nothing. His slogan: syntax is not sufficient for semantics.

lessons.orientation: Model a mental state by its causal role, see why one role can have many realisers and weigh Searle's Chinese Room.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two calculators both show 7 when you press 3 + 4. One is built from gears and the other from silicon chips.

intro.promise: By the end you'll run a machine table, say why a mental state could have many physical realisers, and weigh Searle's Chinese Room.
intro.whyItMatters: Whether a machine could think depends on whether a mind is a thing or a pattern of doing.

recap.keyIdea: A mental state can be defined by its role, so one kind can have many realisers. Searle's room asks whether playing the right role is enough for understanding.

blocks.text: You ran Block's drinks machine on three coin sequences and saw that its table never mentions what it is made of. Then you met the room that tests the idea.

recap.nextHook: If a mind is a pattern, what keeps one person the same person over time? Next, personal identity.

lessons.title: What makes you you

steps.headline: Locke: you are the same person as anyone whose experiences you remember from the inside.

lead.text: On the direct reading, a later stage is the same person as an earlier stage just when it remembers that stage's experiences from the inside.
Call this the memory criterion. Your body and your name do not enter into it.
Thomas Reid's brave officer was flogged as a boy and remembers it as an officer. As an old general he remembers taking the standard, but not the flogging.
Apply the criterion to each earlier stage separately.

reveal.text: You applied the criterion pair by pair. The general passes for the officer and fails for the boy, though the officer passes for the boy.

steps.headline: Show that the direct memory criterion contradicts itself in Reid's case.

workedSteps.text: The general remembers the officer's deed, so the criterion says the general is the officer.
The officer remembers the flogging, so the criterion says the officer is the boy.
Identity passes along a chain: if the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, the general is the boy. But he remembers nothing of the flogging, so the criterion says he is not.

lead.text: Reid's case gives general = officer and officer = boy, but general ≠ boy. If a is b and b is c, then a is c. Ask what that rule of identity is called.

reveal.text: That rule is transitivity, and the direct criterion violates it, so it cannot be a criterion of identity. The usual repair counts overlapping chains of memory: continuity rather than direct connection.

steps.headline: Four stages: A aged 10, B aged 30, C aged 50 and D aged 80. Each remembers only the stage before it.

workedSteps.text: A and B are linked by memory. B and C are linked. C and D are linked.
On the continuity view, count every later stage the chain reaches from A.

lead.text: Suppose each half of your brain is transplanted into a different body, and each survivor remembers your past equally well. Psychological continuity does not care which body holds the memories.

reveal.text: Two people satisfy the criterion, but they are not one another, so they cannot both be you. Continuity theorists add a non-branching clause. Parfit concluded that identity is not what matters; Relation R, psychological connectedness and continuity, is.

lead.text: A scanner records every cell, destroys your body on Earth and builds an exact replica on Mars that remembers your life. The bodily criterion says you are wherever the same living body continues.
Parfit's branch-line case adds a twist: the scanner fails to destroy you, so you and the replica both exist.

reveal.text: No body continues to Mars, so on the bodily criterion the replica is a new person. A psychological criterion says you travelled.

lessons.orientation: Apply Locke's memory criterion, Reid's transitivity objection and Parfit's fission and teleporter cases.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Ann is the same person as Bea. Bea is the same person as Cy.

intro.promise: By the end you'll apply Locke's memory criterion, say why Reid's case breaks it, then test fission and teleporter cases.
intro.whyItMatters: Questions about copying, memory loss and survival all depend on what makes a person the same person over time.

recap.keyIdea: The direct memory criterion breaks the transitivity of identity, so the continuity view counts chains of memory. Fission and teleporters then pull psychological and bodily criteria apart.

blocks.text: You applied the memory criterion to Reid's general and saw it contradict itself. Then you counted a chain from age 10 to 80 and followed a split brain and a scanner.

recap.nextHook: Now to ethics. Next, how to count the consequences of what we do.

lessons.title: Counting consequences

steps.headline: Expected utility weights each outcome's value by its probability.

lead.text: Consequentialism judges an act by its outcomes. When the outcomes are uncertain, multiply each outcome's value by its probability and add.
The total is the act's expected utility.
Option B has two outcomes. Weight each value by its probability and add, then compare the total with the sure 50.

reveal.text: You weighed the gamble: 0.6 × 100 + 0.4 × 0 comes to more than the sure 50. An expected-utility maximiser takes the gamble; a cautious agent might not.

steps.headline: A treatment gives 10 units of benefit with probability 0.7 and causes 20 units of harm with probability 0.3. Is it worth giving?

workedSteps.text: Give the harm a negative value.
Weight each outcome by its probability.
Add them. The total is positive, so the treatment beats doing nothing, which scores 0.

steps.headline: A vaccination programme gives 20 units of benefit with probability 0.9 and causes 30 units of harm with probability 0.1. Should it run?

reveal.text: Mill's greatest happiness principle supplies the values: acts are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. He also held that some pleasures are higher: better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

workedSteps.text: Weight the benefit: probability 0.9 times 20 units.
Weight the harm as a negative: probability 0.1 times −30 units.
Add the weighted values.

lead.text: Philippa Foot posed the trolley case in 1967, and Judith Jarvis Thomson recast it. A utilitarian counts lives and nothing else.

reveal.text: Pulling the lever saves four lives net. Most people judge that pulling is permitted, so the utilitarian verdict and common opinion agree here. The next lesson shows a case where they part.

cases.label: Five ahead, one on the side
Three ahead, one on the side

lead.text: T. M. Scanlon imagined Jones, trapped and receiving painful shocks. Freeing him means cutting a broadcast that millions are watching, for an hour.
Summed, the viewers' small losses can outweigh Jones's suffering. Ask which feature of utilitarianism produces that verdict.

reveal.text: That feature is aggregation: summing welfare across people. Critics say it ignores the separateness of persons.

lessons.orientation: Rank acts by their expected outcomes, and see where summing welfare across people gives troubling verdicts.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You are offered a coin flip. Heads wins you £100. Tails wins you nothing. You can play it again and again.

intro.promise: By the end you'll rank acts by expected utility, count harms as negatives, and see where adding up welfare across people gives troubling verdicts.
intro.whyItMatters: Policies and rescues are decided under uncertainty. Expected utility is a standard way to compare them.

recap.keyIdea: A consequentialist ranks acts by expected utility, weighting every outcome by its probability, with harms as negatives. Adding welfare across people can then outvote one person's great harm.

blocks.text: You weighed a coin flip, a vaccination and a treatment. Then you counted the net lives saved by the lever and met the transmitter room.

recap.nextHook: The lever and the footbridge save the same number of lives. Next, why many people judge them differently.

lessons.title: Duty, persons and the footbridge

steps.headline: To use someone as a means is to make them part of how your plan works.

lead.text: If the plan would fail without a person's body or effort, you are using that person as a means.
If the plan would work just as well without them there, their harm is a side effect.
Judith Jarvis Thomson's variant puts you on a footbridge beside a heavy stranger. Compare it with the switch: count the deaths if you do nothing and if you act.

reveal.text: The arithmetic matches the switch case, yet most people judge that pushing is wrong. A theory that only counts outcomes cannot tell the cases apart.

steps.headline: Apply the idea of a means to the footbridge push.

workedSteps.text: State the plan: the stranger's body will stop the trolley.
Ask whether the plan works without him. It fails, so his death is how it works.
Treating a person that way, as a tool and not as a person, is what Kant's formula forbids.

steps.headline: Name Kant's formulation about how to treat persons.

workedSteps.text: Kant says: treat people always as ends, and never merely as a means.
This is called the formula of ___.

lead.text: A maxim is the rule you act on. Kant asks whether you could will everyone to act on yours.
Take a false promise to repay a loan. Universal false promising would make every promise unbelievable, so the maxim defeats itself.

reveal.text: That is the formula of universal law: act only on a maxim you can at the same time will to become a universal law. The test is not that universal lying has bad results, but that the maxim cannot be consistently universalised. Such commands are categorical: they bind whatever you want.

premises.text: My maxim: when I need money, I will promise to repay it, knowing I cannot.
If everyone acted on this maxim, no one would believe a promise to repay.
If no one believed such promises, the maxim could not be acted on.

conclusion.text: I cannot will the maxim as a universal law, so the false promise is forbidden.

premises.text: My maxim: when I borrow money, I will repay it as promised.
If everyone acted on this maxim, promises to repay would remain credible.

conclusion.text: I can will this maxim as a universal law.

lead.text: Some philosophers allow a foreseen harm as a side effect of a good act, yet forbid intending harm as a means. That permits the switch and forbids the footbridge.
Thomson's loop case strains it.

reveal.text: This is the doctrine of double effect, traced to Aquinas: an act with a foreseen bad effect is permitted only if the good outweighs it and the bad effect is not intended as an end or as a means.

lessons.orientation: Apply Kant's universal-law and humanity formulations, and compare the switch and footbridge cases.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Case A: you pull a lever, and a trolley that would kill five people kills one person on a side track instead.
Case B: you push a heavy stranger off a footbridge, and his body stops the trolley.

intro.promise: By the end you'll apply Kant's tests, tell a harm used as a means from a side effect, and say why the footbridge feels different.
intro.whyItMatters: Many moral rules, such as promises and consent, are about how we treat people, not how many we save.

recap.keyIdea: Kant's tests ask how we treat people, not only how many we save. Using a person as a means is forbidden, and a maxim that cannot be universalised is ruled out.

blocks.text: You counted four lives saved in the footbridge case, asked whether the plan needed the stranger's body, and tested a false promise by imagining everyone making it.

recap.nextHook: Not every ethic looks at acts or rules. Next, Aristotle on character and the mean.

lessons.title: Character and the mean

steps.headline: A virtue lies between a vice of deficiency and a vice of excess.

lead.text: Each virtue concerns a sphere of feeling or action. Courage concerns fear and confidence, with cowardice and rashness on either side.
Aristotle's mean is relative to us: it depends on the person and the situation.
Aristotle supposes that ten minae of food is too much for an athlete and two minae too little. The arithmetic mean is the number halfway between them.

reveal.text: You found the arithmetic midpoint. Aristotle's point is that a trainer will not order that amount for everyone: it would be too little for the wrestler Milo and too much for a beginner.

steps.headline: Place courage for a trained firefighter and for an untrained passer-by.

workedSteps.text: Sphere: fear and confidence. Cowardice has too little confidence and rashness has too much.
The firefighter's right band sits higher on the scale than the passer-by's.
So courage is a mean relative to us, not one fixed point on the scale.

steps.headline: Place generosity between its two vices.

workedSteps.text: Sphere: giving and taking money.
Excess: prodigality, giving too much.
Name the vice of deficiency, giving too little.

lead.text: Aristotle contrasts virtues of thought with virtues of character, and says they are acquired differently. For character he points to learning to build or to play the lyre.

reveal.text: Virtues of character come from habit: we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones. A beginner's courage occupies a different band from a veteran's because practice reshapes what each can rightly face.

lead.text: Return to Aristotle's own example and measure it. On a scale from 2 to 10 minae, the arithmetic midpoint is fixed. The mean relative to us moves, and for a beginner it sits below the midpoint.

reveal.text: Practical wisdom, phronesis, is the capacity to see where the mean lies in a particular case. Its aim is eudaimonia, often translated happiness or flourishing: living well, in activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

model.sphere: eating, for an athlete in training
eating, for an athlete in training

lessons.orientation: Locate a virtue between two vices, distinguish the mean relative to us from an arithmetic midpoint, and see how virtue is acquired.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A drill of 20 laps is too much for a beginner and too little for a champion.

intro.promise: By the end you'll place a virtue between two vices and tell Aristotle's mean from a midpoint.
intro.whyItMatters: Courage and generosity are matters of degree, and the right degree depends on who you are.

recap.keyIdea: A virtue is a mean between two vices, and the mean is relative to us. It is not the arithmetic midpoint, and it is acquired by habit.

blocks.text: You found the midpoint of Aristotle's scale and saw why it fails for Milo and for a beginner. You placed generosity between its vices and measured a beginner's band.

recap.nextHook: Last, a question about the whole of society: what would you choose if you did not know your place in it?

lessons.title: The social contract

steps.headline: A social contract justifies government by what free people would agree to.

lead.text: Start from the state of nature: life with no government at all.
Then ask what free and equal people would agree to, to leave it. Different answers give different governments.
One philosopher argued that people are roughly equal in their power to kill one another. Competition, fear and pride then drive them into a war of every man against every man.
Name the philosopher who drew this picture.

reveal.text: That is Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651). Rational people would covenant to obey a sovereign to escape it. Locke's state of nature already has a law of nature, so his government rests on the consent of the governed and keeps limits.

premises.text: Without a common power, each person may do whatever preserves himself.
Even the weakest can kill the strongest, by plot or alliance.
Competition, fear and pride make conflict likely.

conclusion.text: Without a sovereign, life is a war of all against all.

premises.text: In the state of nature a law of nature already forbids harming others.
People leave it only to secure their lives, liberties and property.

conclusion.text: Government is legitimate only by consent, and only within those limits.

steps.headline: Behind the veil of ignorance, you choose without knowing your place.

lead.text: John Rawls asks which principles you would choose for society if a veil of ignorance hid your place in it: your class, talents and conception of the good.
With no basis for probabilities, he argued, you would use maximin: choose the option whose worst outcome is best.
Society A pays its three equal groups different incomes. If you are equally likely to land in any group, your expected income is the average of the three.

reveal.text: You averaged the three incomes. Society B's average comes to 30, so on averages alone A looks better.

steps.headline: Compare society A (10, 40, 70) with society C (20, 45, 95) by the average and by maximin.

workedSteps.text: Averages: A is 120 ÷ 3 = 40. C is 160 ÷ 3, about 53.
Worst positions: A pays its lowest group 10 and C pays 20.
C wins on both rules, so there is no dilemma between them here.

lead.text: Maximin looks only at each society's worst position. Compare the lowest income in each.

reveal.text: B's worst-off group gets 25 and A's gets 10, so maximin picks B even though A has the higher average. John Harsanyi and others argued that a rational chooser would maximise expected utility, which picks A.

lead.text: Real societies do not split into equal groups. When a quarter of people are in one position and three quarters in another, weight each income by its share.

reveal.text: Maximin ignores the shares and looks only at the worst position, which is the strongest objection to it. Rawls's difference principle, its institutional cousin, permits inequalities only when they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.

lessons.orientation: Compare Hobbes's and Locke's social contracts, then choose principles behind Rawls's veil of ignorance with maximin and averages.

intro.whyItMatters: Arguments about taxes, rights and welfare often ask what a fair society would look like from anyone's seat.

recap.keyIdea: Contract theories ask what people would agree to. Behind the veil, averages and maximin can choose differently.

blocks.text: You averaged incomes for three societies and found where average and worst case agree and part. You also saw how Hobbes and Locke answer why we obey.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.' How many premises does this argument state?
hints: Find the claim the passage wants you to accept; that is the conclusion.
'Since' introduces the reasons. List each separate claim it introduces.
Count the claims offered as reasons, leaving out the conclusion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the bridge's date of construction, and the rule that bridges of that age must be inspected this year. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Two premises support one conclusion. The “since” clause holds both reasons, and the final clause is the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the conclusion. Count only the claims offered as reasons for it.
Look at the “and” in the “since” clause. It joins two separate claims, each offered as a reason.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the conclusion of: 'The council should not sell the playing field. After all, it is the only open space in the ward, and selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's own planning policy.'?
hints: Ask which sentence the others are offered to support.

acceptedIdeas: The council should not sell the playing field
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'After all' introduces the reasons, so the opening sentence is the claim they support.

choices.label: The council should not sell the playing field
The field is the only open space in the ward
Selling a ward's only open space breaks planning policy

questions.onCorrect: “After all” announces reasons, so the opening sentence is the claim they support.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are reasons offered for the claim, not the claim itself. Ask which sentence the others support.

questions.prompt: What is the traditional name for an argument that leaves one of its premises unstated?
hints: The term comes from Greek and is used of everyday arguments that skip an obvious step.
It begins with 'enthy-'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enthymeme: an argument with a suppressed premise, such as 'Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree'.

questions.onCorrect: An enthymeme is an argument with a suppressed premise, such as Mira's.

misconceptions.feedback: A syllogism has both premises stated. The name you want is for an argument that leaves one out.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Water expands when it freezes, so a full, sealed glass bottle left in the freezer will crack; and a cracked bottle leaks, so the freezer will need cleaning.' How many conclusions, intermediate and final, does it draw?
hints: Each 'so' introduces a conclusion.
A conclusion can be used again as a premise for a later step.
Count every claim that follows a 'so'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two. The bottle will crack (concluded from expansion), and the freezer will need cleaning (concluded from the crack and the leak).

questions.onCorrect: Two conclusions: the bottle will crack, and the freezer will need cleaning. The first becomes a premise for the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the last claim. The earlier “so” also draws a conclusion.
Check what follows each “so”. The water expanding is a reason, not something concluded.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Because all reptiles are cold-blooded and every snake is a reptile, and because cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun, snakes bask in the morning sun.' How many premises does it state?
hints: Find the conclusion first; it comes at the end.
Each 'because' clause can contain more than one claim joined by 'and'.
Count the separate claims offered as reasons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three premises: reptiles are cold-blooded; snakes are reptiles; cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Three premises. A single “because” clause can hold two claims, and the final clause is the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the conclusion at the end. Count only the claims offered as reasons.
A “because” clause with “and” holds two claims, and there is a second “because” after it. Count every reason.

questions.prompt: In 'We should cancel the picnic, since the forecast says thunderstorms', which single word signals the premise?
hints: Look for the word that could be replaced by 'because'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Since' introduces the reason, the forecast; the conclusion is that we should cancel.

questions.onCorrect: “Since” introduces the reason, the forecast. The conclusion is what the reason supports.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are parts of the claims. Look for the small word that points at the reason.

questions.prompt: Premises: 'If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet' and 'The pavement is wet'. Conclusion: 'It rained overnight'. Is the argument valid or invalid?
hints: Look for a possible situation in which both premises are true and the conclusion is false.
Could the pavement be wet for some other reason?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Invalid: a burst water main on a dry night makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid: wet pavement has other causes, so the premises can be true with a false conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for another way the pavement could be wet. If there is one, the premises do not force the conclusion.

questions.prompt: For the form 'p → q, q, so p', in how many of the four truth-table rows are both premises true?
hints: List the four rows: TT, TF, FT, FF for p and q.
The second premise, q, removes every row where q is false.
Check p → q in the rows that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both premises are true when p and q are both true, and when p is false and q true. In the second of those rows the conclusion is false.

questions.onCorrect: Two rows keep both premises true, and in one of them the conclusion is false.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every row. The second premise rules some out.
Check the row with p false and q true. Are both premises true there?

questions.prompt: In 'All metals are magnetic; copper is a metal; so copper is magnetic', which premise is false? Answer with its number, 1 or 2.
hints: Validity is not in question here; check each premise against the facts.
Is copper a metal?
Does a fridge magnet stick to a copper pipe?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Premise 1 is false: copper is a metal but is not attracted by a magnet. The argument is valid and unsound.

questions.onCorrect: Premise 1 is false, and the argument is still valid. Validity does not depend on the facts.

misconceptions.feedback: Copper is a metal, which is all premise 2 says. Check the other premise against the facts.

questions.prompt: How many of the eight truth-table rows are counterexamples to 'p → q, r → q, so p → r'?
hints: Start from the conclusion: when is p → r false?
In those rows, which value of q makes the first premise true?
Check the second premise in the row that remains.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The conclusion is false only when p is true and r false. Then p → q needs q true, and r → q is true because r is false. One row: p true, q true, r false.

questions.onCorrect: One row: p and q true, r false. That single counterexample shows the form invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion fails when p is true and r false. Check whether both premises survive there.
Fix p true and r false. Only one value of q can then keep the first premise true.

questions.prompt: A valid argument has a false conclusion. What must be the case?
hints: Suppose every premise were true. What would validity then require?

acceptedIdeas: At least one premise is false
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If every premise were true, validity would force a true conclusion. So at least one premise is false, though not necessarily all.

choices.label: At least one premise is false
The argument is not valid after all

questions.onCorrect: At least one premise must be false. If all were true, validity would force a true conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: Only one false premise is needed. The others may be true.
The argument is stated to be valid. Ask what validity requires if the conclusion is false.

questions.prompt: A complete truth table for an argument with four different atomic sentences has how many rows?
hints: One atomic sentence gives two rows, true and false.
Each new atomic sentence doubles the number of rows.
Calculate 2 raised to the power of the number of atomic sentences.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each atomic sentence doubles the rows: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

questions.onCorrect: Each atomic sentence doubles the rows: four sentences give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the table for three atomic sentences. A fourth doubles it again.
That is how many sentences there are. Each one doubles the rows.

questions.prompt: Dr Okafor argues that a bridge design is unsafe. A councillor replies: 'She once lost a contract to that firm, so we can ignore her.' Name the fallacy.
hints: Does the reply engage with the reasons about the bridge, or with something else?
The fallacy has a Latin name meaning 'to the person'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ad hominem: the reply targets the arguer's history instead of her calculations.

questions.onCorrect: Ad hominem: the reply targets the arguer's history instead of her calculations.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply does not misstate her view. Look at what it attacks instead.

questions.prompt: Ana: 'Speed limits beside schools should drop to 20 mph.' Ben: 'Ana wants every car in the country crawling along at 20, which would wreck the economy.' Name Ben's fallacy.
hints: Compare Ana's actual proposal with the one Ben criticises.
The fallacy is named after a figure that is easy to knock down.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straw man: Ben attacks a national limit that Ana never proposed.

questions.onCorrect: A straw man: Ben attacks a national limit that Ana never proposed.

misconceptions.feedback: Ben does not attack Ana herself. Compare her proposal with the one he criticises.

questions.prompt: 'A feather is light. Whatever is light is not dark. So a feather is not dark.' Name the fallacy.
hints: Ask whether 'light' means the same thing in both premises.
The fallacy's name comes from Latin for 'equal voice': one word, two senses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equivocation: 'light' means 'not heavy' in one premise and 'pale' in the other.

questions.onCorrect: Equivocation: “light” shifts from “not heavy” to “pale” between the premises.

misconceptions.feedback: The slip is inside the words. Check whether “light” keeps one meaning throughout.

questions.prompt: Someone says: 'Smoking causes cancer, so you shouldn't smoke.' Which added premise gives the most charitable reconstruction?
hints: Choose the premise that is believable and still connects the reason to the conclusion.

acceptedIdeas: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is plausible and makes the argument valid. The other two are false or much stronger than the speaker needs.

choices.label: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease
Anything that causes something bad should be banned

questions.onCorrect: The believable premise makes the argument valid and worth answering. Charity picks the strongest version.

misconceptions.feedback: That premise is false, so it makes the argument easy to dismiss. Charity looks for one a thoughtful speaker would accept.
That is much stronger than the speaker needs. Charity does not add more than the argument requires.

questions.prompt: 'This newspaper never prints falsehoods. We know this because its front page says so, and that statement must be true, since the paper never prints falsehoods.' Name the fallacy.
hints: Trace where the support for 'never prints falsehoods' comes from.
The argument travels in a circle back to its starting claim.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Begging the question: the conclusion is used to support the premise offered for it.

questions.onCorrect: Begging the question: the claim is used to support the very statement offered for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage offers no choice between options. Trace where its support for the claim comes from.

questions.prompt: 'Either we close the library or the council goes bankrupt.' The council in fact has several other ways to save money. Name the fallacy.
hints: Count the options the speaker offers, then the options that really exist.
The fallacy is named after a forced choice between two horns.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A false dilemma: two options are presented as the only ones when others exist.

questions.onCorrect: A false dilemma: two options are presented as the only ones when others exist.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing is assumed in a premise here. Count the options offered against those that exist.

questions.prompt: Gettier's first case: Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket. He concludes 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket'. In fact Smith gets the job and, unknown to him, has ten coins himself. How many of the three JTB conditions does his belief meet?
hints: List the conditions: truth, belief and justification.
Check truth against what actually happened, not against Smith's evidence.
Check whether his reasons were good ones when he formed the belief.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three. The belief is true and Smith believes it, having inferred it from strong evidence. That is why the case troubles the analysis.

questions.onCorrect: Three: true, believed and justified. That is why the case troubles the analysis.

misconceptions.feedback: Check truth against what happened. Smith does get the job and does have ten coins.
His evidence was strong when he formed the belief. Check each condition separately.

questions.prompt: Ana looks at a usually reliable station clock reading 2:15 and believes it is 2:15. It is 2:15, but the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago. On the JTB analysis, does Ana know the time? Answer yes or no.
hints: Apply the analysis mechanically: check each of its three conditions.
The question asks what the analysis says, not what intuition says.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes on the JTB analysis, since the belief is true, held and justified. Most people judge that she does not know, which is the problem for the analysis.

questions.onCorrect: On the analysis, yes: the belief is true, held and justified. Most people judge that she does not know.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what intuition says. The question asks what the analysis says, so check its three conditions mechanically.

questions.prompt: Gettier cases show that justified true belief is not ___ for knowledge. Fill the gap with 'necessary' or 'sufficient'.
hints: In a Gettier case, are all three conditions present?
If they are present and knowledge is absent, what do they fail to guarantee?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sufficient: all three conditions hold in a Gettier case, yet the subject does not know.

questions.onCorrect: Sufficient: all three conditions hold in a Gettier case, yet the subject does not know.

misconceptions.feedback: Gettier did not dispute that each condition is needed. Ask whether having all three guarantees knowledge.

questions.prompt: Henry drives through a county full of barn facades and looks at the only real barn. Could his true belief 'that is a barn' easily have been false? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine Henry glancing at a different building along the same road.
Would his evidence have looked any different?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. Had he looked at any of the facades he would have formed the same belief, and it would have been false. The belief is not safe.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Any of the facades would have produced the same belief, so his belief is not safe.

misconceptions.feedback: Imagine Henry glancing at a different building along the same road. Would his evidence look any different?

questions.prompt: The no-false-lemmas reply says Smith's reasoning in the coins case passed through a false belief. Which one?
hints: Find the step in Smith's reasoning that did not match what happened.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Smith reasoned from 'Jones will get the job', which is false. The other two claims are true.

choices.label: Smith has ten coins in his pocket
The man who will get the job has ten coins

questions.onCorrect: Smith reasoned from “Jones will get the job”, which is false. The other claims are true.

misconceptions.feedback: That claim is true. Find the step in his reasoning that did not match what happened.

questions.prompt: Who published the three-page paper 'Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?' in 1963?
hints: The cases that bear his name answer the paper's question.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Edmund Gettier, in Analysis, 1963.

questions.onCorrect: Edmund Gettier, in 1963: his three-page paper gave the cases their name.

misconceptions.feedback: Those philosophers gave other cases. The 1963 paper is by the author whose name the cases bear.

questions.prompt: Premises: 'If I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived by a demon' and 'I do not know I am not deceived by a demon'. Conclusion: 'I do not know I have hands'. Valid or invalid?
hints: Write it as p → q, ¬q, so ¬p.
Is there a row in which both premises are true and ¬p is false?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid. The form is modus tollens: p → q, ¬q, so ¬p.

questions.onCorrect: Valid: the form p → q, ¬q, so ¬p is modus tollens, and it has no counterexample row.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and the conclusion false. Does one exist?

questions.prompt: Which philosopher answered the sceptic in 1939 by holding up his hands and arguing from 'here is one hand' to the existence of an external world?
hints: He was a Cambridge philosopher famous for defending common sense.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: G. E. Moore, in 'Proof of an External World'.

questions.onCorrect: G. E. Moore, in “Proof of an External World”: he trusted his hands over the sceptic's premise.

misconceptions.feedback: That philosopher belongs to another part of the story. The 1939 reply with raised hands came from a Cambridge champion of common sense.

questions.prompt: For the form 'p → q, ¬q, so ¬p', in how many of the four truth-table rows are both premises true?
hints: The premise ¬q keeps only the rows in which q is false.
In those rows, check where p → q is true.
A conditional with a true antecedent and false consequent is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the row with p false and q false. There ¬p is true, so the form has no counterexample.

questions.onCorrect: One row keeps both premises true, and ¬p holds in it. The form has no counterexample.

misconceptions.feedback: The premise ¬q rules out the rows where q is true. Check which of the rest keep p → q true.
¬q removes every row where q is true. Count only what remains.

questions.prompt: Dretske and Nozick hold that you know you have hands but cannot know you are not a handless brain in a vat. Which principle about knowledge must they reject?
hints: Their two verdicts together contradict a general principle linking known claims to what they entail.
The principle says knowledge is 'closed' under known entailment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Closure: the principle that knowledge carries over to what you know your knowledge entails.

questions.onCorrect: Closure: knowledge carries over to what you know your knowledge entails.

misconceptions.feedback: Think of a principle linking what you know to what it entails, not a rule of logic.

questions.prompt: What does Descartes' all-powerful deceiver, a deceiving God or evil demon, put in doubt that his dream argument leaves standing?
hints: Ask which beliefs would stay true even inside a dream.

acceptedIdeas: Simple truths of arithmetic, such as two and three making five
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Descartes notes that two and three make five whether he wakes or sleeps. An all-powerful deceiver could make him err even there.

choices.label: Simple truths of arithmetic, such as two and three making five

questions.onCorrect: Even awake or asleep, two and three make five. A demon could falsify such truths too.

misconceptions.feedback: Dreams already put such beliefs in doubt. Ask what would stay true even inside a dream.

questions.prompt: In the Second Meditation, what did Descartes take to survive even the demon's deception? Answer in two words.
hints: Even a deceiver needs someone to deceive.
The claim concerns the thinker himself.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'I exist': whatever deception he suffers, he must exist to be deceived.

questions.onCorrect: “I exist”: to be deceived at all, he must exist.

misconceptions.feedback: A deceiver could fake all of that. Ask what Descartes must be in order to be deceived.

questions.prompt: 1,000 people are screened. 10% have the condition. The test is positive for 90% of people with it and for 10% of people without it. What percentage of people who test positive have the condition?
hints: Find how many of the 1,000 have the condition, and how many of those test positive.
Find how many of the healthy people test positive.
Divide the ill positives by all positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 are ill and 90 of them test positive. 900 are well and 90 of them test positive. 90 of 180 positives are ill: 50%.

questions.onCorrect: 50%. Half of the positives are ill, far below the test's hit rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate among the ill. The question asks what share of all positives are ill.
That is the false-alarm rate. Divide the ill positives by all positives.

questions.prompt: The same test (90% hit rate, 10% false alarms) is used on 1,000 people, of whom 1% have the condition. How many people test positive in total?
hints: Find the number who are ill, then the number of them the test catches.
Apply the false-alarm rate to everyone who is well.
Add the two groups of positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 are ill and 9 test positive. 990 are well and 99 test positive. 9 + 99 = 108.

questions.onCorrect: 108 positives. A rare condition produces mostly false alarms, which are 99 of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the ill people the test catches. Add the healthy people it flags.
That counts only the false alarms. Add the ill people the test catches.

questions.prompt: A test is positive for 90% of people with a condition and for 10% of people without it. By what factor does a positive result multiply the odds that someone has the condition?
hints: The factor is the likelihood ratio.
Compare P(positive | condition) with P(positive | no condition).
Divide the hit rate by the false-alarm rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The likelihood ratio is 0.9 / 0.1 = 9, so posterior odds are nine times the prior odds.

questions.onCorrect: A factor of 9. The likelihood ratio is the hit rate divided by the false-alarm rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between the two rates. The likelihood ratio compares them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Of 1,000 people, 10% have a condition. A test catches 80% of cases and is positive for 5% of people without the condition. What percentage of positives have the condition?
hints: Count the ill people the test catches.
Count the healthy people it flags.
Divide true positives by all positives and convert to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 true positives and 0.05 × 900 = 45 false positives. 80 / 125 = 64%.

questions.onCorrect: 64%: 80 true positives out of 125 positives in all.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of true positives. Express it as a share of all positives.
That is the number of false alarms. Divide the true positives by all positives.

questions.prompt: P(H) = 0.2, P(E | H) = 0.5 and P(E | not-H) = 0.25. Find P(H | E), as a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Find the probability of E and H together.
Find the probability of E without H, using P(not-H) = 1 − P(H).
Divide the first by the sum of both.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The joint probability of E and H is 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1; of E without H, 0.8 × 0.25 = 0.2. So P(H | E) = 0.1 / (0.1 + 0.2) = 1/3.

questions.onCorrect: A third: the ill positives divided by all positives, counted group by group.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P(E | H), the hit rate. Weigh it by how likely H was, then compare with the other route to E.
That is the joint probability of E and H. Divide it by the probability of E overall.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the error of judging P(H | E) from P(E | H) while ignoring how common H was to begin with? Two words are enough.
hints: The neglected quantity is the prior: how often H holds in the population.
Statisticians call that frequency the '___ rate'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Base-rate neglect, also called the base-rate fallacy.

questions.onCorrect: Base-rate neglect: ignoring how common the hypothesis was before the evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: Those describe the test. The neglected quantity is how common the condition was to begin with.

questions.prompt: 'Lois believes Superman can fly. Lois does not believe Clark Kent can fly. So Superman is not Clark Kent.' The premises are true in the story and the conclusion is false. Is the argument valid or invalid?
hints: Recall the definition: can the premises be true while the conclusion is false?
The story itself supplies the situation you need.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Invalid: true premises with a false conclusion is exactly a counterexample. 'Being believed by Lois to fly' is not a property that Leibniz's law carries across.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid: both premises are true in the story and the conclusion is false.

misconceptions.feedback: The story itself supplies the situation: Superman is Clark Kent. Can both premises be true while the conclusion is false?

questions.prompt: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked Descartes how an unextended mind could move an extended body. What is this objection to substance dualism called? Answer in one or two words.
hints: The problem concerns causation running between mind and body.
Its name describes the two substances acting on each other.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The interaction problem: how two substances with nothing in common could causally affect each other.

questions.onCorrect: The interaction problem: how substances with nothing in common could causally affect each other.

misconceptions.feedback: That names a different issue. Elisabeth asked how two such different substances could act on each other.

questions.prompt: Elisabeth's argument as 'p → q, q → r, ¬r, so ¬p' has eight truth-table rows. In how many are all three premises true?
hints: Start with ¬r: keep only rows where r is false.
Among those, q → r needs q to be false.
Then check p → q with q false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ¬r leaves the rows with r false; q → r then needs q false; p → q then needs p false. One row remains, and ¬p is true in it.

questions.onCorrect: One row keeps all three premises true, and ¬p holds in it. The argument is valid.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many rows ¬r keeps. The other two premises remove more.
Check q → r where r is false: it needs q false. Then check p → q.

questions.prompt: U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart held that each type of mental state, such as pain, is a type of brain state. Name their view.
hints: The view says mental states and brain states are not two things but one.
Its name uses the relation expressed by 'is the same thing as'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mind-brain identity theory, also called type physicalism.

questions.onCorrect: The identity theory: each type of mental state is a type of brain state.

misconceptions.feedback: Their view says the mental and the physical are not two things but one.

questions.prompt: Which statement is Leibniz's law, the indiscernibility of identicals?
hints: The law goes from identity to properties, not the other way.

acceptedIdeas: If x is identical with y, then x and y share every property
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leibniz's law runs from identity to shared properties. The converse, from shared properties to identity, is the identity of indiscernibles.

choices.label: If x is identical with y, then x and y share every property
If x and y share every property, then x is identical with y
No two distinct things share any property

questions.onCorrect: Leibniz's law runs from identity to shared properties, never the other way.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs from shared properties to identity. Leibniz's law starts from identity.
That is far stronger than Leibniz's law. It says distinct things never share any property.

questions.prompt: Name the view that there is only one kind of substance, physical, but that mental properties are not physical properties.
hints: It is a form of dualism, but not about substances.
The duality lies in the properties things have.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Property dualism.

questions.onCorrect: Property dualism: one physical substance, with mental properties that are not physical ones.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for the view that allows one substance yet says mental properties differ.

questions.prompt: Ned Block's drinks machine sells a can for 20p, takes 10p and 20p coins and starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 10p, then 10p, then 10p. How many cans come out?
hints: Track the state after each coin: nothing owed or 10p credited.
A can comes out only when the total reaches 20p.
Count the coins that complete a 20p total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10p sets a credit; the second 10p completes 20p and releases a can; the third sets a new credit. One can.

questions.onCorrect: One can: the first 10p sets a credit, the second buys a can, the third starts a new credit.

misconceptions.feedback: A can comes out when the credit reaches 20p. Track the state after each coin.
Not every coin buys a can. Track the state after each one.

questions.prompt: The same machine starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 20p, then 10p, then 20p. How many cans come out?
hints: A 20p coin with nothing owed buys a can immediately.
Track the credit left after each coin.
A 20p coin with 10p already credited overpays by 10p but still buys a can.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20p buys a can at once; 10p sets a credit; 20p with 10p credited buys a can and returns 10p. Two cans.

questions.onCorrect: Two cans: the first 20p buys one at once, and the last 20p buys another after the 10p credit.

misconceptions.feedback: A 20p with 10p already credited overpays by 10p but still buys a can.
The 10p in the middle only sets a credit. Track the state after each coin.

questions.prompt: Name the thesis, used by Putnam against the identity theory, that a single mental kind such as pain can be realised in very different physical systems.
hints: Think of pain in humans, octopuses and possible robots.
The thesis says one kind can be 'realised' in many ways.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiple realisability.

questions.onCorrect: Multiple realisability: one mental kind, many physical realisers.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a theory about mental states. The thesis wanted says one kind can be realised in many ways.

questions.prompt: Searle says the man in the room understands no Chinese. Name the reply that the whole room, including the man, the rulebook and the papers, understands.
hints: The reply moves understanding from the man to something larger.
It is named after what the man, the book and the papers form together.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The systems reply.

questions.onCorrect: The systems reply: understanding belongs to the whole room, not to the man alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That names the thought experiment or another reply. The one wanted moves understanding from the man to something larger.

questions.prompt: Two machines, one of gears and one of silicon chips, share the same machine table and receive the same coins. Do they end in different functional states? Answer yes or no.
hints: A functional state is defined by its place in the table.
Does the table mention gears or chips?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Functional states are fixed by the table, which is identical; only the realisers differ.

questions.onCorrect: No. The table is identical, so the functional states are too. Only the realisers differ.

misconceptions.feedback: A functional state is fixed by its place in the table. Does the table mention gears or chips?
