questions.prompt: What conclusion does Searle draw from the Chinese Room?
hints: Searle grants that the room's replies are fluent.

acceptedIdeas: Running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Searle grants the behaviour. He denies that implementing the program is enough for understanding.

choices.label: Running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding
No computer can ever behave as if it understands
Only biological brains can run programs

questions.onCorrect: Searle grants the fluent behaviour and denies that running a program is enough for understanding.

misconceptions.feedback: Searle grants that the room's replies are fluent. His claim is about what running a program amounts to.
He makes no claim about which things can run programs. His claim is about what running one amounts to.

questions.prompt: Reid's brave officer: the officer remembers being flogged as a boy; the old general remembers taking the standard as an officer but has forgotten the flogging. On Locke's direct memory criterion, with how many of the two earlier stages is the general identical?
hints: The direct criterion counts only what a stage itself remembers.
Check the officer stage, then the boy stage.
Count the earlier stages the general remembers from the inside.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One: the officer, whose actions he remembers. He does not remember the boy's flogging, so on the direct criterion he is not the boy.

questions.onCorrect: One: the officer, whose actions he remembers. He does not remember the flogging.

misconceptions.feedback: He remembers the officer's deed but not the boy's flogging. Check each earlier stage separately.
He does remember the officer's actions from the inside.

questions.prompt: Reid's case yields general = officer and officer = boy, but general ≠ boy. Which logical property of identity does the direct memory criterion violate?
hints: Look at how the three equations chain together.
The property lets you pass along a chain of identities.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Transitivity: if a = b and b = c, then a = c.

questions.onCorrect: Transitivity: if a is b and b is c, then a is c.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at how the three equations chain together. The property lets you pass along a chain.

questions.prompt: Each half of your brain is transplanted into a new body, and both survivors remember your past equally well. On a psychological continuity criterion with no extra clause, how many future people are continuous with you?
hints: Psychological continuity does not care which body holds the memories.
Count the survivors who remember your past from the inside.
Each survivor is a separate candidate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both survivors are psychologically continuous with you, so two people satisfy the criterion. Identity is one-one, which is the problem.

questions.onCorrect: Two survivors are continuous with you, so identity, which is one-to-one, cannot follow continuity.

misconceptions.feedback: Continuity does not care which body holds the memories. Count every survivor who remembers your past.

questions.prompt: A teleporter destroys your body on Earth and builds an exact replica on Mars that remembers your life. On the bodily criterion of personal identity, do you survive? Answer yes or no.
hints: The bodily criterion asks whether the same living body continues.
What happened to the body on Earth?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. No body continues from Earth to Mars, so on the bodily criterion the replica is a new person.

questions.onCorrect: On the bodily criterion you do not survive: no body continues to Mars.

misconceptions.feedback: The bodily criterion asks whether the same living body continues. What happened to the body on Earth?

questions.prompt: Stage A is a child of 10. B, aged 30, remembers A's experiences; C, aged 50, remembers B's but not A's; D, aged 80, remembers C's but not B's or A's. On the continuity view, which counts overlapping chains of memory, how many of B, C and D are the same person as A?
hints: Continuity follows chains, not just direct links.
Trace the links from A forward.
Count every later stage the chain reaches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three: A–B, B–C and C–D are linked, so the chain connects each later stage to A.

questions.onCorrect: Three: each link joins a later stage to the one before, so the chain connects all of them to the first.

misconceptions.feedback: Continuity follows chains, not just direct links. Trace each link forward from the first stage.

questions.prompt: In Parfit's branch-line case the scanner copies you to Mars but fails to destroy your body on Earth. Which survivor does the bodily criterion count as you?
hints: Follow the body, not the memories.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the person on Earth has your body. The replica has psychological continuity without bodily continuity.

questions.onCorrect: The person on Earth: only that person has your body. The replica has psychological continuity only.

misconceptions.feedback: The replica has your memories but not your body. The bodily criterion follows the body.
Only one of them has your living body. The bodily criterion follows the body.

questions.prompt: Option B gives a 60% chance of 100 welfare units and a 40% chance of 0. What is its expected utility, in welfare units?
hints: Multiply each outcome's value by its probability.
The failure outcome contributes nothing.
Add the weighted values.
questions.onCorrect: 60 units: 0.6 × 100 plus nothing, which beats the sure 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the success value. Weight it by its probability.
That is the weight on failure, not the expected value. Weight the success value by its probability.

questions.prompt: A programme gives 20 units of benefit with probability 0.9 and causes 30 units of harm with probability 0.1. What is its expected utility?
hints: Give the harm a negative value.
Weight each outcome by its probability.
Add the two weighted values.
questions.onCorrect: 15 units: a weighted benefit of 18 less a weighted harm of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the benefit's weighted value. The harm still has to be subtracted.
Harm counts against the programme. Give it a negative value.

questions.prompt: A runaway trolley will kill five people on the main track unless you pull a lever sending it onto a side track, where it will kill one. Counting lives only, how many more people survive if you pull?
hints: Count the deaths if you do nothing.
Count the deaths if you pull.
Subtract.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Not pulling: five die. Pulling: one dies. 5 − 1 = 4 more survive.

questions.onCorrect: Four more survive: five die if you do nothing, one if you pull.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deaths if you do nothing. Subtract the death if you pull.
That adds the deaths. You are comparing two options, not totalling them.

questions.prompt: Scanlon's transmitter room: a utilitarian may let Jones suffer an hour of shocks rather than interrupt a broadcast, because millions of small losses add up. Name the feature of utilitarianism that produces this verdict.
hints: Ask how utilitarianism combines the viewers' losses.
The word for adding many small quantities into one total.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aggregation: summing welfare across people, so many small losses can outweigh one great harm.

questions.onCorrect: Aggregation: many small losses can add up to outweigh one great harm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the theory, but not the feature in question. Ask how the viewers' losses are combined.

questions.prompt: Who wrote that it is 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'?
hints: The line defends higher pleasures within utilitarianism.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mill, in chapter II of Utilitarianism (1861), defending a distinction between higher and lower pleasures.

questions.onCorrect: Mill, in Utilitarianism (1861), defending higher and lower pleasures.

misconceptions.feedback: Bentham counted the quantity of pleasure. Mill added a distinction between higher and lower.
Kant defends duties that do not depend on outcomes. The line comes from a utilitarian.

questions.prompt: Policy X gives three people +4, +4 and −5 welfare units. Policy Y gives each of them +2. By how many units does Y's total exceed X's?
hints: Add the effects of X across the three people.
Add the effects of Y.
Subtract X's total from Y's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: X totals 4 + 4 − 5 = 3. Y totals 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. 6 − 3 = 3 units.

questions.onCorrect: Three units: Y totals 6 and X totals 3. Aggregation sums welfare across people.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Y's total. Compare it with X's total.
Y's total is the larger one. Subtract X's from Y's.

questions.prompt: From a footbridge you could push a heavy stranger onto the track; his body would stop a trolley that will otherwise kill five. Counting lives only, how many more people survive if you push?
hints: Count deaths if you do nothing.
Count deaths if you push.
Subtract.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Not pushing: five die. Pushing: the stranger dies. 5 − 1 = 4, the same as the switch case.

questions.onCorrect: Four more survive: five die if you do nothing, one if you push. The count matches the switch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deaths if you do nothing. Subtract the death if you push.
That adds the deaths. You are comparing two options, not totalling them.

questions.prompt: Kant's formulation that you must never treat a person merely as a means is called the formula of ___. Fill the gap with one word.
hints: Kant says we must treat it, in ourselves and others, always as an end.
The word names what all persons share, in Kant's sense of rational nature.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The formula of humanity.

questions.onCorrect: The formula of humanity: persons are always to be treated as ends.

misconceptions.feedback: That is another formulation. The one about persons is named after what all persons share.

questions.prompt: Kant tests the maxim 'make a false promise to get a loan' by asking whether it could hold for everyone; universal false promising would make such promises impossible. Which formulation of the categorical imperative is this?
hints: The test imagines the maxim adopted by everyone.
Its name says the maxim must be able to become a law for all.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The formula of universal law.

questions.onCorrect: The formula of universal law: could the maxim hold for everyone?

misconceptions.feedback: That formulation concerns how to treat persons. This test imagines the maxim adopted by everyone.

questions.prompt: Name the doctrine, traced to Aquinas, that may permit a foreseen harm as a side effect of a good act but forbids intending harm as a means.
hints: One act, two effects: one intended, one merely foreseen.
Its name counts the effects.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The doctrine of double effect.

questions.onCorrect: The doctrine of double effect: a foreseen side effect may be permitted, an intended means may not.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the doctrine. Its name counts the effects of one act.

questions.prompt: 'If you want to be trusted, keep your promises.' What kind of imperative is this, in Kant's terms?
hints: Does the command depend on a goal you happen to have?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It binds only someone who has the stated goal of being trusted, so it is hypothetical. A categorical imperative binds whatever you want.

questions.onCorrect: Hypothetical: it binds only someone who wants to be trusted. A categorical imperative binds whatever you want.

misconceptions.feedback: A categorical imperative binds whatever you want. This one depends on a goal.
Universal names a formulation, not a kind of imperative.

questions.prompt: In Thomson's loop case the side track rejoins the main line, so only the one person's body stops the trolley. Is that person's death a means or a side effect of saving the five?
hints: Ask whether the plan would still work if the one person were absent.
If the plan needs his body, his death is part of how it works.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A means: if the one were not on the loop, the trolley would come round and kill the five.

questions.onCorrect: A means: if the one were absent, the trolley would come round and kill the five.

misconceptions.feedback: Ask whether the plan would still work if he were absent. If it needs his body, his death is part of how it works.

questions.prompt: Aristotle supposes that ten minae of food is too much and two minae too little. What amount, in minae, is the arithmetic mean of the two?
hints: The arithmetic mean lies halfway between the two amounts.
Add the two amounts.
Halve the sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (2 + 10) / 2 = 6 minae. Aristotle's point is that the mean relative to us need not be this amount.

questions.onCorrect: Six minae: halfway between two and ten. Aristotle's mean relative to us need not be that amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the two amounts. The mean lies halfway, so halve it.
That is the gap between the two amounts. The midpoint lies halfway between them.

questions.prompt: Generosity concerns giving money. Its vice of excess is prodigality. Name its vice of deficiency.
hints: The deficient person gives too little and takes too much.
Think of the everyday word for someone who will not spend.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meanness, also translated stinginess or illiberality.

questions.onCorrect: Meanness, also translated stinginess or illiberality: giving too little.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the excess, or belongs to another virtue. Name the fault of giving too little.

questions.prompt: According to Aristotle, do we acquire virtues of character mainly by teaching or by habit?
hints: Aristotle compares virtue with learning to build or to play the lyre.
Teaching produces virtues of thought; something else produces virtues of character.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By habit: we become brave by doing brave acts.

questions.onCorrect: By habit: we become brave by doing brave acts.

misconceptions.feedback: Teaching mainly produces virtues of thought. Think of how you learn to build.

questions.prompt: On a scale from 2 to 10 minae of food, a beginner's right amount runs from 3 to 5 minae. How many minae below the arithmetic mean of the scale is the top of the beginner's range?
hints: Find the midpoint of the whole scale first.
The top of the beginner's range is its larger number.
Subtract the top of the range from the midpoint.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The arithmetic mean is (2 + 10) / 2 = 6 minae. The top of the beginner's range is 5, which is 6 − 5 = 1 mina below it.

questions.onCorrect: One mina below: the midpoint of the scale is 6 and the top of the beginner's range is 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Find the midpoint of the scale first. Then subtract the top of the range from it.
The range's top lies below the midpoint, so take it away from the midpoint, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: Ten minae is too much and two too little. For Milo, a champion wrestler, Aristotle says six minae would be:
hints: Milo is a champion athlete with a large body to feed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Too little. Aristotle says six would be too little for Milo and too much for a beginner.

questions.onCorrect: Too little for Milo, who is a champion with a large body to feed.

misconceptions.feedback: Six is only the arithmetic midpoint. Milo needs more than that.
Milo is a champion with a large body to feed. Ask whether six would be generous for him.

questions.prompt: What Greek word, often translated 'happiness' or 'flourishing', names the highest human good for Aristotle?
hints: It begins with the Greek prefix for 'good'.
Its second part is daimon, a guiding spirit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eudaimonia: living well and doing well, an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

questions.onCorrect: Eudaimonia: living well, an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

misconceptions.feedback: That is another Greek term. The one wanted names the highest good, often translated flourishing.

questions.prompt: Who wrote that, without a common power, the life of man would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'?
hints: He wrote Leviathan during the English Civil War.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), chapter 13.

questions.onCorrect: Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), describing life without a common power.

misconceptions.feedback: That philosopher belongs to the story, but is not the author of this line. Think of the author of Leviathan.

questions.prompt: Society A pays its three equal-sized groups 10, 40 and 70 income units. If you are equally likely to land in any group, what is your expected income in A?
hints: Each group has probability one third.
Add the three incomes.
Divide by the number of groups.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (10 + 40 + 70) / 3 = 40 income units.

questions.onCorrect: 40 income units: the three incomes added and divided by three.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the top group's income. Add all three incomes and divide.
That is the total. Divide by the number of groups.

questions.prompt: Behind the veil you choose between society A (10, 40, 70) and society B (25, 30, 35), three equal groups each. Which society does the maximin rule choose? Answer A or B.
hints: Maximin looks only at each society's worst position.
Compare the lowest income in each society.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Society B: its worst-off group receives 25, against 10 in A.

questions.onCorrect: Society B: its worst-off group gets more than A's, and maximin looks only at the worst position.

misconceptions.feedback: Maximin ignores the average. Compare the lowest income in each society.

questions.prompt: In society D, a quarter of people receive 30 income units and three quarters receive 50. What is the average income?
hints: Weight each income by the share of people who receive it.
Multiply 30 by a quarter and 50 by three quarters.
Add the two weighted amounts.
questions.onCorrect: 45 income units: each income weighted by the share of people who receive it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average if the groups were equal. Weight each income by its share.
That is the two incomes added. Weight each by its share of the people.

questions.prompt: Locke held that legitimate political power rests on the ___ of the governed. Fill the gap with one word.
hints: Locke's citizens make themselves members of a society by their own act.
The word for agreeing to something.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Consent: people leave the state of nature by agreeing to form a political society.

questions.onCorrect: Consent: people leave the state of nature by agreeing to form a political society.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of Locke's picture, but not what legitimacy rests on. Think of agreeing to something.

questions.prompt: Rawls's difference principle permits social and economic inequalities only when:
hints: The principle is the institutional cousin of maximin.

acceptedIdeas: They work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inequalities must benefit the least advantaged, and attach to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity.

choices.label: They work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged
Everyone receives exactly the same income

questions.onCorrect: Inequalities must work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, the cousin of maximin.

misconceptions.feedback: Rawls does not require equal incomes. Inequalities are allowed under a condition.
Raising the average is the utilitarian aim. The difference principle asks about the least advantaged.

questions.prompt: How many people in the town test positive in all?
hints: The test flags people in two groups. How many in each?
One group is the 100 who have the condition. The other is the 900 who do not.
Add the people flagged in both groups.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 90 of the ill and 90 of the well are flagged: 90 + 90 = 180.

questions.onCorrect: 180 flags come from two groups. Counting both is the first step in weighing a test result.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one group. The test flags people who are ill and people who are well.
That is how many have the condition. Count everyone who tests positive.

questions.prompt: A condition affects 1 person in 100. Before any test, what is your prior that you have it?
hints: The prior is set before the evidence arrives.

choices.label: The chance of a positive result

questions.onCorrect: The prior is the starting probability, here set by how common the condition is.

misconceptions.feedback: The hit rate describes the test. The prior is how likely the hypothesis was before testing.
A positive result is the evidence. The prior comes before it.

questions.prompt: Why divide by all the positives, not only the ill ones?
hints: Ask what group the question is about.

acceptedIdeas: The question asks what share of those who test positive are ill.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The question asks what share of those who test positive are ill.

choices.label: The question asks what share of those who test positive are ill.
The ill people are the majority.

questions.onCorrect: The posterior is about everyone who tests positive, so the false alarms belong in the total.

misconceptions.feedback: In this town the ill people are a minority. The reason lies in what the question asks.
False alarms are part of the positives. They change the answer.

questions.prompt: A test is positive for 90% of ill people and 10% of healthy ones. Half of 1,000 people are ill. What percentage of positives are ill?
hints: Split the 1,000 into ill and well, then count the flagged in each.
Find how many of the ill test positive, and how many of the well do.
Divide the ill positives by all positives and convert to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 ill, of whom 450 test positive. 500 well, of whom 50 test positive. 450 ÷ 500 = 90%.

questions.onCorrect: Common conditions change the answer: with half the town ill, most positives are real.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the prior. Count how many ill people the test catches and how many healthy people it flags.
That is the false-alarm rate. Divide the ill positives by all positives.

questions.prompt: About how much, in pounds, do you win per play on average?
hints: Heads comes up only some of the time.
How often does heads come up over many plays?
Take that share of £100, and add what tails pays.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Heads half the time pays £100, tails half the time pays nothing: 0.5 × 100 = 50.

questions.onCorrect: £50 a play. Weighting each outcome by how often it happens is the idea behind expected utility.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what heads pays, but heads comes up only some of the time.
Tails pays nothing, but heads pays a lot. Weight each by how often it comes up.

questions.prompt: A gamble gives a 50% chance of 10 units and a 50% chance of 20 units. What is its expected utility?
hints: Weight each value by its probability, then add.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 15 units

questions.onCorrect: Half of 10 plus half of 20: each outcome counts in proportion to its probability.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two values without weighting them. Each counts only half the time.
That is only the lower outcome. Expected utility weights both outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why is the harm written as −20?
hints: What should a harm do to the total?

acceptedIdeas: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.

choices.label: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.
So that the probabilities add to 1.

questions.onCorrect: Harm counts against the act, so it enters with a negative value.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign shows direction, not importance. A harm pulls the total down.
The probabilities already add to 1. The sign is about the value of the outcome.

questions.prompt: Option A gives an 80% chance of 50 units and a 20% chance of −10 units. What is its expected utility?
hints: Give each outcome its probability weight.
The bad outcome has a negative value, so it pulls the total down.
Add the two weighted values.
questions.onCorrect: 38 units. The small chance of harm trims the total, but only in proportion to its probability.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the bad outcome. Weight it and add it as a negative.
That adds the harm instead of subtracting it. The value is negative.

questions.prompt: Is the neighbour's reply a reason about the canteen at all? Answer yes or no.
hints: What does the reply say about vegetables on the menu?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. It says something about Jo, not about whether the canteen should serve more vegetables.

questions.onCorrect: The reply is about Jo, not the canteen. A good reply to an argument speaks to its reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply is about Jo. Ask what it would say if someone else made the same suggestion.

questions.prompt: “You can trust the report, because the report says it is trustworthy.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
hints: Compare the claim with the reason given for it.

acceptedIdeas: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.

choices.label: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.

questions.onCorrect: The reason just repeats the claim. An argument that assumes its conclusion adds no support.

misconceptions.feedback: No options are being offered here. Look at how the reason relates to the claim.
Nobody is attacked. Compare the claim with the reason given for it.

questions.prompt: Why does Kit's reply leave Sam's proposal untouched?
hints: Compare what Sam proposed with what Kit criticises.

acceptedIdeas: It attacks a different, more extreme position.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It attacks a different, more extreme position.

choices.label: It attacks a different, more extreme position.
It is spoken in a rude tone.
It gives no reasons at all.

questions.onCorrect: Kit's criticism may be good, but it aims at a position Sam never took.

misconceptions.feedback: Tone is not the fault. Compare what Sam proposed with what Kit criticises.
Kit does give a reason. The reason is aimed at the wrong target.

questions.prompt: Lena argues for longer library hours. Rob replies: “Lena wants the library open all night, every night, which would bankrupt us.” Name Rob's fallacy.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straw man: Rob attacks an extreme version of Lena's proposal.

questions.onCorrect: Rob swaps in a more extreme view and refutes that. The restated proposal is what to answer.

misconceptions.feedback: Rob does not attack Lena herself. Compare her proposal with the one he criticises.

questions.prompt: Both calculators show 7. Are they both adding? Answer yes or no.
hints: What makes something an adder: its parts, or what it does with its inputs?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. Adding is what each does with 3 and 4, whatever its parts are.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. What counts is what each does with its inputs, whatever it is built from.

misconceptions.feedback: Both turn the same inputs into the same output by following the same rules. Does it matter what the parts are made of?

questions.prompt: In the drinks machine, what does “10p credited” mean?
hints: The table says what each state does, not what it is made of.

acceptedIdeas: The state that turns a further 10p into a can
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The state that turns a further 10p into a can

choices.label: The state that turns a further 10p into a can
A particular metal part inside the machine
A 10p coin sitting in the tray

questions.onCorrect: The state is defined by its role in the table: what it does with the next coin.

misconceptions.feedback: The table never mentions parts. A state is defined by what it does next.
A coin is an input, not a state. The state is defined by what it does with the next input.

questions.prompt: Why does the machine's response to a 10p depend on its state?
hints: Compare what a 10p does from nothing owed with what it does from 10p credited.

acceptedIdeas: The same coin does different things in different states.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same coin does different things in different states.

choices.label: The same coin does different things in different states.
Coins vary from one to the next.
It counts how many cans it has sold.

questions.onCorrect: The table pairs each state with each input. The same coin can start a credit or complete a sale.

misconceptions.feedback: Every 10p is treated alike. Compare what it does in different states.
The table does not track cans sold. It tracks the state the machine is in.

questions.prompt: The machine starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 20p, 20p, 10p, 10p. How many cans come out?
hints: Track the state after each coin.
A 20p with nothing owed buys a can at once.
The two 10p coins together make 20p.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each 20p buys a can at once, and the two 10p coins together buy a third: 3 cans.

questions.onCorrect: Three cans. The table gives every coin sequence its output without reference to the machine's parts.

misconceptions.feedback: The last two coins also make 20p between them. Track the state after each.
The 10p coins buy a can only together. Track the state after each coin.

questions.prompt: Did Tess know that the coin would land heads? Answer yes or no.
hints: Ask what Tess had to go on.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Her guess was right, but she had no reason for it.

questions.onCorrect: A right answer reached by luck is not knowledge. Something more than being right has to be in place.

misconceptions.feedback: A guess can be right without being known. Ask what Tess had to go on.

questions.prompt: A man holds a well-reasoned belief that turns out to be false. Which of the three conditions fails?
hints: He holds the belief, and he had reasons for it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Truth

questions.onCorrect: A false claim cannot be known, whatever the reasons. Truth is the condition that fails.

misconceptions.feedback: He does hold the belief. Check the condition that depends on how things are.
His reasoning was good, which is stated. Check the condition that depends on how things are.

questions.prompt: Why is Ravi's case different from Smith's coins case?
hints: Compare what Ravi's evidence is about with what Smith's was about.

acceptedIdeas: His evidence is connected to the fact that makes his belief true.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: His evidence is connected to the fact that makes his belief true.

choices.label: His evidence is connected to the fact that makes his belief true.

questions.onCorrect: Ravi's reason is the very rain that makes his belief true. Smith's reason was about someone else.

misconceptions.feedback: Smith's evidence was strong too. Compare what each person's evidence is about.
Seeing the rain makes the belief secure. The difference lies in what the evidence is about.

questions.prompt: A man is certain his lottery ticket will win, though he has nothing to go on. It does win. Which of the three conditions is missing? Answer in one word.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Justification: his belief is true and held, but he had no good reason for it.

questions.onCorrect: His belief is true and held. Without a good reason it is a lucky guess, not knowledge.

misconceptions.feedback: His ticket does win, so his belief is true. Check what he had to go on.
He is certain, so he does believe it. Check what he had to go on.

questions.prompt: In which case is a person's body the way you save the five? Answer A or B.
hints: Ask in which case the plan would fail if the one person were not there.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Case B: the stranger's body is what stops the trolley.

questions.onCorrect: In Case B the plan needs the stranger's body. In Case A the one is hit only because the trolley goes that way.

misconceptions.feedback: In Case A the trolley is turned away. Ask in which case the plan would fail if the one person were absent.

questions.prompt: Which of these uses the stranger as a means?
hints: Ask whether the plan would fail without his body.

acceptedIdeas: Pushing him so that his body stops the trolley
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pushing him so that his body stops the trolley

choices.label: Pushing him so that his body stops the trolley
Pulling a lever that turns the trolley, so that it hits him

questions.onCorrect: Only the push needs his body. In the other cases the plan would work without him.

misconceptions.feedback: Without him on the side track the plan would work just as well. His death is a side effect there.
A warning treats him as someone to inform. His body plays no part in the plan.

questions.prompt: Why does needing his body matter?
hints: What does the plan treat him as?

acceptedIdeas: It makes him a tool of the plan.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It makes him a tool of the plan.

choices.label: It makes him a tool of the plan.

questions.onCorrect: If the plan needs his body, he is being used as a tool, which is what the formula forbids.

misconceptions.feedback: The count of lives is the same in both cases. Ask what the plan treats him as.
His weight is only what makes the plan work. Ask what the plan treats him as.

questions.prompt: Maxim: “I will keep a promise only when it suits me.” If everyone acted on it, could promising still work as a practice? Answer yes or no.
hints: Would anyone rely on a promise that is kept only when convenient?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. If promises were kept only when convenient, nobody could rely on them.

questions.onCorrect: Universalised, the maxim destroys the practice it depends on, so it fails Kant's test.

misconceptions.feedback: Ask whether anyone would rely on a promise that is kept only when convenient.

questions.prompt: Does your friend's belief show that Sam and the mayor are different people? Answer yes or no.
hints: Her belief is about what she thinks, not about Sam.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. What she believes about the two names does not change who they pick out.

questions.onCorrect: No. A difference in what she believes is a fact about her, not about Sam or the mayor.

misconceptions.feedback: She has a view about one name and none about the other. Is that a fact about the man, or about her?

questions.prompt: If Clark Kent is Superman, which must be true?
hints: One thing under two names has one set of properties.

acceptedIdeas: Whatever is true of Clark Kent is true of Superman.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whatever is true of Clark Kent is true of Superman.

choices.label: Whatever is true of Clark Kent is true of Superman.
Clark Kent and Superman differ in some property.
Lois believes the same things about both.

questions.onCorrect: One man, one set of properties. What Lois believes is a fact about Lois.

misconceptions.feedback: If they are one man, no property can differ between them. Think of what “one man” means.
Lois may not know they are one man. Her beliefs are facts about her.

questions.prompt: What does the masked-man case suggest about the doubt argument?
hints: Compare “believed by Lois” with “doubted by me”.

acceptedIdeas: “Being doubted by me” may describe my state of mind, not a property of my body.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Being doubted by me” may describe my state of mind, not a property of my body.

choices.label: “Being doubted by me” may describe my state of mind, not a property of my body.
Nothing, because the two cases are unrelated.
That Descartes' conclusion must be false.

questions.onCorrect: Both describe someone's mental state. If so, Leibniz's law cannot carry them across.

misconceptions.feedback: Both arguments have the same shape. Compare “believed by Lois” with “doubted by me”.
The case shows a weakness in the argument. It does not settle what is true.

questions.prompt: “Ben believes Mark Twain wrote Huckleberry Finn. He does not believe Samuel Clemens wrote it. So Mark Twain is not Samuel Clemens.” Valid or invalid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Invalid: Twain was Clemens, and what Ben believes does not change that.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. Mark Twain was Samuel Clemens, so the premises can hold with a false conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: Mark Twain was Samuel Clemens. Can the premises be true while the conclusion is false?

questions.prompt: Must Ann be the same person as Cy? Answer yes or no.
hints: Picture all three names pointing at people. How many people are there?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. Ann is Bea and Bea is Cy, so all three are one person.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Identity passes along a chain, which is why any criterion of identity has to respect it.

misconceptions.feedback: Picture all three names pointing at one person. Can the first and third differ?

questions.prompt: On the direct memory criterion, Anna at 60 is the same person as Anna at 20 only if:
hints: The criterion looks at what a later stage remembers.

acceptedIdeas: she remembers the 20-year-old's experiences from the inside.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: she remembers the 20-year-old's experiences from the inside.

choices.label: she remembers the 20-year-old's experiences from the inside.

questions.onCorrect: The memory criterion asks what the later stage remembers from the inside. Bodies and names do not matter.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bodily criterion. Locke's criterion looks at memory.
A name is not part of the criterion. Look at what the later stage remembers.

questions.prompt: Why is this a problem for the direct memory criterion?
hints: Look at how the three claims chain together.

acceptedIdeas: Identity should pass along a chain, and the criterion breaks that.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Identity should pass along a chain, and the criterion breaks that.

choices.label: Identity should pass along a chain, and the criterion breaks that.

questions.onCorrect: The criterion makes the general the officer and the officer the boy, yet denies the general is the boy.

misconceptions.feedback: Forgetting is not the issue. Look at how the three claims chain together.
Nothing here depends on false memories. Look at how the three claims chain together.

questions.prompt: Each of four stages remembers only the stage just before it. On the direct memory criterion, with how many earlier stages is the last stage identical?
hints: The direct criterion counts only what a stage itself remembers.
Which earlier stage does the last stage remember?
Count the earlier stages it remembers from the inside.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the third stage: it is the only one the last stage remembers directly.

questions.onCorrect: Just one. Direct memory reaches back a single step, which is why the criterion needed chains.

misconceptions.feedback: The last stage does remember the one before it from the inside. Check each earlier stage separately.
Direct memory reaches only the stage just before. Count what it remembers itself.

questions.prompt: Your body is destroyed and an exact replica that remembers your life is built elsewhere. On a psychological criterion, do you survive? Answer yes or no.
hints: Which does a psychological criterion follow: memory and character, or the body?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The replica has your memories and character, which is what that criterion follows.

questions.onCorrect: A psychological criterion follows memory and character, so the replica is you on that view.

misconceptions.feedback: A psychological criterion follows memory and character, and the replica has both.

questions.prompt: How many separate reasons does Maya give for eating early?
hints: Which sentence is the thing she wants us to do?
The rest of what she says is there to back it up. List those claims one at a time.
Count the claims offered as support, leaving out the one they back.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away. “We should eat early” is what they support.

questions.onCorrect: Two reasons back one claim. Seeing which is which is the first move in judging any argument.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the claim Maya wants us to accept. It is what the reasons support, not one of them.
The second sentence joins two claims with “and”. Each is a separate reason.

questions.prompt: In “The shop must be shut, because the lights are off”, which part is the conclusion?
hints: Ask which claim the other part is there to support.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shop must be shut

questions.onCorrect: The shop's being shut is the claim. The lights being off is offered as the reason for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The lights are the reason offered. A conclusion is the claim that a reason supports.
“Because” is an indicator word. It points at a reason; it is not a claim at all.

questions.prompt: Why is the sentence “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet” the conclusion?
hints: What do the other sentences do for it?

acceptedIdeas: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.

choices.label: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
It comes first in the passage.

questions.onCorrect: A conclusion is picked out by what the other claims do for it, not by where it sits.

misconceptions.feedback: Conclusions can come last, as in “since …” passages. Position never settles it; what the other claims do for it does.
Length has nothing to do with it. Look at what the other claims are for.

questions.prompt: Which unstated premise makes “Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree” work as an argument?
hints: The missing premise must link being a solicitor to having a law degree.

acceptedIdeas: Every solicitor has a law degree.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every solicitor has a law degree.

choices.label: Every solicitor has a law degree.

questions.onCorrect: That premise bridges the gap between the reason and the conclusion. Without it the step is a leap.

misconceptions.feedback: That may be true, but it does not connect being a solicitor with having a degree.
That runs the wrong way. It starts from law graduates, but Mira is introduced as a solicitor.

questions.prompt: If the friend's two claims are true, must the conclusion be true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Try to imagine both claims being true while the conclusion fails.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The conclusion follows from the two claims, whether or not they are true.

questions.onCorrect: The shape guarantees the conclusion. Whether the claims are true is a separate question.

misconceptions.feedback: Try it. Suppose you know the shop is open, and you do not know it is unburned. Can both hold?

questions.prompt: Which rule of inference takes p → q and p to q? Answer with its Latin name.
hints: It is the rule that affirms the first part of an “if … then”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Modus ponens.

questions.onCorrect: Modus ponens: from “if p then q” and p, infer q. It has no counterexample row.

misconceptions.feedback: Modus tollens starts from the denial of the second part. Here the second premise affirms the first part.

questions.prompt: Why can Moore's argument and the sceptic's both be valid?
hints: Compare where each argument starts.

acceptedIdeas: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.

choices.label: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.
One of them must be invalid.
Validity is a matter of opinion.

questions.onCorrect: Validity only says the conclusion follows. The quarrel is over which starting point deserves more confidence.

misconceptions.feedback: Both have valid forms. Compare where each one starts.
Validity is settled by the shape. The disagreement is about which premise to accept.

questions.prompt: “If I know I have hands, I know I am not a handless brain in a vat. I know I have hands. So I know I am not a handless brain in a vat.” Valid or invalid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid: it has the form p → q, p, so q.

questions.onCorrect: Valid: the form p → q, p, so q has no counterexample row.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and the conclusion false. Does one exist?

questions.prompt: How many sweets should the smallest pile hold, to give yourself the most?
hints: Whatever piles you make, you receive the smallest one.
What happens to the smallest pile if you make the piles unequal?
Share the 12 sweets so that the smallest pile is as large as it can be.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal piles of 4 make the smallest pile as large as possible: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Equal piles give you the best worst case. Choosing as if you might be anyone leans towards fairness.

misconceptions.feedback: Making the piles unequal only shrinks the one you will receive. Look for the largest smallest pile.
That is the whole stock. There are three piles to fill.

questions.prompt: Why would people in Hobbes's state of nature accept a sovereign?
hints: Think of what life is like with no common power.

acceptedIdeas: To escape a war of all against all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To escape a war of all against all

choices.label: To escape a war of all against all
Because a law of nature already forbids harm

questions.onCorrect: Without a sovereign, fear and competition lead to conflict. Obedience is the way out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Locke's state of nature. Hobbes thought nothing restrains people without a common power.
Kindness plays no part. Think of what life is like with no common power.

questions.prompt: Behind the veil, what do you know?
hints: The veil hides your place in society.

acceptedIdeas: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours

choices.label: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours

questions.onCorrect: You can compare arrangements, but you cannot tilt them towards your own position.

misconceptions.feedback: Income is part of your place in society, which the veil hides.
Talents are part of what the veil hides along with class and your view of the good.

questions.prompt: Why is there no dilemma between A and C?
hints: Compare both numbers for each society.

acceptedIdeas: C does better on the average and for the worst-off.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: C does better on the average and for the worst-off.

choices.label: C does better on the average and for the worst-off.

questions.onCorrect: When one society wins on both rules, the choice is easy. The rules matter only when they disagree.

misconceptions.feedback: Both societies have three groups. Compare both numbers for each society.
Averages are one of the two rules in play. Compare both numbers for each society.

questions.prompt: Society F pays three equal groups 15, 30 and 60. Society G pays them 20, 25 and 30. By how many units does F's average exceed G's?
hints: Find each society's total, then divide by the number of groups.
Find F's average and G's average separately.
Subtract G's average from F's.
questions.onCorrect: F's average is higher by ten units, though its worst-off group does worse. The rules can pull apart.

misconceptions.feedback: That is F's average. The question asks for the gap between the two averages.
That is G's average. The question asks for the gap between the two averages.

questions.prompt: Could both claims be true and yet Priya have left without a badge? Answer yes or no.
hints: Picture Priya at the party. What was true of every guest?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. If every guest got a badge and Priya was a guest, she got one.

questions.onCorrect: No gap is possible. When the claims are true, the conclusion is forced. That is the idea behind validity.

misconceptions.feedback: Try to picture it. Priya is a guest, and every guest was given a badge. Where would the gap be?

questions.prompt: What shows that an argument is invalid?
hints: Think of what validity rules out.

acceptedIdeas: A possible situation with true premises and a false conclusion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A possible situation with true premises and a false conclusion

choices.label: A possible situation with true premises and a false conclusion

questions.onCorrect: A counterexample is exactly that situation. One is enough to show invalidity.

misconceptions.feedback: Valid arguments can have false premises. Invalidity needs a situation where the premises are true and the conclusion false.
Surprise is a feeling. Validity is about whether the premises can all hold while the conclusion fails.

questions.prompt: Why does the row-by-row test settle whether the form is valid?
hints: A counterexample must be one of the rows.

acceptedIdeas: It covers every way the premises could come out true.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It covers every way the premises could come out true.

choices.label: It covers every way the premises could come out true.
It checks whether the premises are true in real life.
It tests only the most likely row.

questions.onCorrect: A counterexample would have to appear among the rows, so a complete table settles validity.

misconceptions.feedback: The rows are possibilities, not facts. Validity does not depend on what is actually the case.
Every row counts, including unlikely ones. A single bad row is enough.

questions.prompt: “All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly.” Is this argument valid? Answer yes or no.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. If both premises were true, the conclusion would have to be. The first premise is false, so it is unsound.

questions.onCorrect: Valid: true premises would force the conclusion. The false first premise makes it unsound.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity ignores whether the premises are true. Suppose both were true: would the conclusion have to be?

questions.prompt: Is there one right number of laps for everyone? Answer yes or no.
hints: Think of a beginner and a champion doing the same drill.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The right amount depends on the person.

questions.onCorrect: The right amount depends on the person. That is the thought behind a mean relative to us.

misconceptions.feedback: Think of a beginner and a champion doing the same drill. Would the same number suit both?

questions.prompt: Courage lies between which two vices?
hints: Courage concerns fear and confidence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cowardice and rashness

questions.onCorrect: Too little confidence is cowardice and too much is rashness. Courage lies between.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are feelings, not vices of deficiency and excess. Courage concerns fear and confidence.
Those are traits of the body. The vices of courage are about fear and confidence.

questions.prompt: Why do the firefighter's and the passer-by's bands differ?
hints: Both bands are for the same virtue on the same scale.

acceptedIdeas: The right amount depends on the person and the situation.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right amount depends on the person and the situation.

choices.label: The right amount depends on the person and the situation.

questions.onCorrect: Training changes what each person can rightly face. The mean is relative to us.

misconceptions.feedback: Firefighters feel fear too. The difference lies in what each can rightly face.
The scale is the same for both. The bands differ because the people do.

questions.prompt: On a scale from 4 to 12 units of food, a champion's right range runs from 10 to 11 units. How many units above the arithmetic mean of the scale is the bottom of that range?
hints: Find the midpoint of the whole scale first.
The bottom of the champion's range is its smaller number.
Subtract the midpoint from the bottom of the range.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The arithmetic mean is (4 + 12) ÷ 2 = 8. The bottom of the range is 10, which is 10 − 8 = 2 above it.

questions.onCorrect: Two above. The champion's mean sits above the midpoint, as the beginner's sits below it.

misconceptions.feedback: Find the midpoint of the whole scale first, then compare it with the bottom of the range.
That is the midpoint of the scale. The question asks how far the bottom of the range is above it.

flashcards.front: In 'The film was dubbed, so it was not shown in its original language; anything not shown in its original language loses some jokes, hence the film lost some jokes', how many words mark a conclusion?
flashcards.back: Two: 'so' and 'hence'. The first marks an intermediate conclusion, the second the final one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'so' and 'hence'. The first marks an intermediate conclusion, the second the final one.

flashcards.front: Name the kind of argument in which one premise is left unstated.
flashcards.back: An enthymeme.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enthymeme.

flashcards.front: What is a valid argument whose premises are all true called?
flashcards.back: A sound argument: valid, with every premise true, so its conclusion is true as well.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A sound argument: valid, with every premise true, so its conclusion is true as well.

flashcards.front: How many counterexample rows does 'p ∨ q, ¬p, so q' have in its four-row truth table?
flashcards.back: None. Both premises are true only when p is false and q true, and there q is true. The form, disjunctive syllogism, is valid.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None. Both premises are true only when p is false and q true, and there q is true. The form, disjunctive syllogism, is valid.

flashcards.front: Name the fallacy of rejecting an argument because of some fact about the person who offers it.
flashcards.back: Ad hominem.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ad hominem.

flashcards.front: Name the principle of reconstructing an opponent's argument in its most plausible form before criticising it.
flashcards.back: The principle of charity.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The principle of charity.

flashcards.front: In a standard Gettier case, how many of the three conditions of the justified-true-belief analysis fail?
flashcards.back: None fail. All three hold, yet the subject does not know; that is what makes it a Gettier case.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None fail. All three hold, yet the subject does not know; that is what makes it a Gettier case.

flashcards.front: Name the condition, proposed in response to Gettier, that a known belief could not easily have been false.
flashcards.back: Safety: in nearby situations where the subject believes it, the belief is true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Safety: in nearby situations where the subject believes it, the belief is true.

flashcards.front: Name the principle: if you know p, and know that p entails q, then you know q.
flashcards.back: The closure principle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The closure principle.

flashcards.front: Name the modern sceptical scenario in which a scientist keeps a brain alive and feeds it experiences by computer.
flashcards.back: The brain in a vat.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The brain in a vat.

flashcards.front: A hypothesis starts at odds of 1 to 1. Evidence is three times as likely if it is true as if it is false. What is the posterior probability, as a percentage?
flashcards.back: Posterior odds are 3 to 1, which is a probability of 3/4 = 75%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Posterior odds are 3 to 1, which is a probability of 3/4 = 75%.

flashcards.front: Name the theorem that gives P(H | E) from P(E | H), P(H) and P(E).
flashcards.back: Bayes' theorem.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bayes' theorem.

flashcards.front: Which philosopher held that the mind is a thinking, unextended substance distinct from the extended body?
flashcards.back: René Descartes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: René Descartes.

flashcards.front: Name the principle that if x is identical with y, then x and y have exactly the same properties.
flashcards.back: Leibniz's law, the indiscernibility of identicals.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leibniz's law, the indiscernibility of identicals.

flashcards.front: Who devised the Chinese Room argument against strong artificial intelligence (1980)?
flashcards.back: John Searle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: John Searle.

flashcards.front: In the 20p drinks machine, 10p is already credited and someone inserts a 20p coin. How many pence of change come out?
flashcards.back: 20p plus the 10p credit is 30p for a 20p can, so 10p change.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20p plus the 10p credit is 30p for a 20p can, so 10p change.

flashcards.front: Who held that personal identity reaches as far back as consciousness can be extended to past actions?
flashcards.back: John Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, chapter 27.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: John Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, chapter 27.

flashcards.front: Who argued from fission and teleporter cases that identity is not what matters in survival?
flashcards.back: Derek Parfit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Derek Parfit.

Which philosopher wrote that nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure?
flashcards.back: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789).

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789).

flashcards.front: What kind of imperative, in Kant's terms, binds you whatever your desires or goals?
flashcards.back: A categorical imperative.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A categorical imperative.

flashcards.front: A switch case has three people ahead and one on the side track. Counting lives only, how many more survive if you divert the trolley?
flashcards.back: 3 − 1 = 2 more survive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 − 1 = 2 more survive.

flashcards.front: In Aristotle's ethics, what is the vice of deficiency for courage?
flashcards.back: Cowardice: too much fear and too little confidence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cowardice: too much fear and too little confidence.

flashcards.front: What Greek term does Aristotle use for the practical wisdom that discerns the mean in a particular case?
flashcards.back: Phronesis.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Phronesis.

flashcards.front: Name Rawls's device that hides your place in society from you while you choose principles of justice.
flashcards.back: The veil of ignorance, part of the original position.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The veil of ignorance, part of the original position.

flashcards.back: E's worst-off group gets 12 and F's gets 15. Maximin chooses F, whose lowest income is 15.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: E's worst-off group gets 12 and F's gets 15. Maximin chooses F, whose lowest income is 15.
